The interpretation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ (1)

Says the Exalted One: The command of Allah has come, that is, it has drawn near to you, O people, and approached, so do not seek to hasten its occurrence.

Then the people of interpretation differed about what the command was, which Allah informed His servants would come and draw near to them, and what it is. Some of them said: it refers to His obligations and His rulings.

Those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾, he said: the rulings, the prescribed punishments, and the obligations.

Others said: rather, it is a warning from Allah to those who associate partners with Him, informing them that the Hour has drawn near and that their punishment has arrived at its appointed time and drawn close.

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: When this verse was revealed, namely ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾, some of the hypocrites said to one another: This man claims that the command of Allah has come, so refrain from some of what you have been doing until you see what will occur. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then there was revealed ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near to them, while they are heedless and turning away﴾. They said: This man claims something similar too. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then there was revealed ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a specified community, they will surely say: What holds it back? Is it not that on the day it comes to them, it will not be turned away from them, and what they used to mock will surround them﴾.

Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Isma'il, from Abu Bakr ibn Hafs, who said: When ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, they raised their heads, so there was revealed ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Shu'ayb narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu Sadiq recite ﴿O My servants, the command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾.

The more correct of the two views in my opinion is the view of those who said: it is a threat from Allah to the people of disbelief in Him and His Messenger, and an announcement from Him to them that the punishment and destruction are near to them. This is because He followed it with His saying, Glory be to Him and exalted is He, ﴿above what they associate with Him﴾, which indicates His rebuke of the polytheists and His warning to them. Moreover, it has not reached us that any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hastened the obligations before they were enjoined upon them, so that it would be said to them on account of that: the obligations of Allah have come to you, so do not hasten them. As for those among the polytheists who sought hastened punishment, they were many.

His saying, Glory be to Him and exalted is He, ﴿above what they associate with Him﴾, means: He, may He be exalted, is declared free of and exalted above the partnership that the Quraysh and whoever among the Arabs was upon their same religion adhered to.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of His saying ﴿above what they associate with Him﴾. The people of Madina and some of the Basrans and Kufans recited ﴿ya'shikun﴾ with the letter ya', as a report about the people of disbelief in Allah, and directing the address of hastening to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); and they recited the second with ya' likewise. The majority of the Kufan readers recited it with ta' (tuʼshikun), directing the address of ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the phrase ﴿above what they associate with Him﴾ to the polytheists. However, the recitation with ta' in both places, as an address to the polytheists, is more correct, for the reason I have explained in the interpretation: that this is a warning from Allah to the polytheists, beginning the start of the verse with their threat and closing its end with a rebuke of their conduct and a magnification of their disbelief, in the form of direct address to them.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whomever of His servants He wills, [saying]: Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me﴾ (2)**

The readers (qurra') differed over the recitation of His saying ﴿yunazzilu al-malā'ikata﴾. The majority of the readers of Madina and Kufa recited ﴿yunazzilu al-malā'ikata﴾ with a *ya'* and a doubled *zay* and with *al-malā'ikata* in the accusative, meaning that God sends down the angels with the Spirit. Some of the Basran and some of the Makkan readers recited *yunzilu al-malā'ikata* with a *ya'* and a single *zay* and with *al-malā'ikata* in the accusative. It is related from some of the Kufans that he recited *tanazzalu al-malā'ikatu* with a *ta'* and a doubled *zay* and with *al-malā'ikatu* in the nominative, though there is a variant report from him, and it is also related from him that he agreed with the rest of the readers of his city.

The most correct recitation in my view is that of the one who recites ﴿yunazzilu al-malā'ikata﴾, meaning: God sends down angels. I chose this because God is the One who sends down His angels with His revelation to His messengers, so attributing the act to Him is more appropriate and more fitting. I preferred *yunazzilu* with the doubled *zay* over the single one, because He, may He be remembered, used to send down revelation to whomever He sent it, one thing after another, and the doubled form, given that this is its meaning, is more appropriate than the single form.

The meaning of the statement is: God sends down His angels with that by which the truth is made alive and falsehood is extinguished, from His command, ﴿upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾, meaning upon whichever of His messengers He wills, ﴿that warn﴾. The first *an* is in the genitive position, as a continuation of "the Spirit," and the second *an* is in the accusative position, governed by *andhirū*. The meaning of the statement is: He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, [commanding]: Warn My servants of My punishment for their disbelief in Me and their association of others with Me, by taking gods and idols alongside Me. "Indeed there is no god but Me," meaning: divinity is fitting only for Me, and nothing other than Me is suitable to be worshipped. "So fear Me," meaning: beware of Me by performing My obligations, devoting worship to Me alone, and making lordship sincerely Mine, for that is your salvation from destruction.

Those who interpret the Qur'an said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Mu'āwiyah narrated to me, from 'Alī, from Ibn 'Abbās, regarding His saying ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit﴾: he said: with the revelation.

- Muḥammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbās, regarding His saying ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾: he said: He sends down the angels [with the same meaning as what came before, from the narration of al-Muthannā from Ibn 'Abbās, as this author habitually does in many places].

- Muḥammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abū 'Āṣim narrated to us, saying: 'Īsā narrated to us. And al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: Warqā' narrated to us. And al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abū Ḥudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us. And al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allāh narrated to us, from Warqā', all of them, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding God's saying ﴿with the Spirit from His command﴾: that no angel descends except that with him is a spirit.

- Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Mujāhid said: His saying ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command﴾: no angel descends except that with him is a spirit. ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾: [he said:] with prophethood. Ibn Jurayj said: I heard that the Spirit is a creation of the angels, and the Spirit descended with it. [Compare] ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is from the command of my Lord﴾.

- Al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allāh narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabī' ibn Anas, regarding His saying ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command upon whomever of His servants He wills, [saying]: Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me﴾: he said: Every word that our Lord speaks is a spirit from Him. [Compare] ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ … to His saying ﴿Surely to God all matters return﴾.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Sa'īd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His saying ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command﴾: he said: He sends down with mercy and revelation from His command, ﴿upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾, so He chooses from among them messengers.

- Muḥammad ibn 'Abd al-A'lā narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatādah, ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾: he said: with revelation and mercy.

As for His saying ﴿that warn: indeed there is no god but Me, so fear Me﴾, we have already explained its meaning.

Those who interpret the Qur'an said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Sa'īd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His saying ﴿that warn: indeed there is no god but Me, so fear Me﴾: God only sent the messengers so that God would be declared One alone, His command would be obeyed, and His wrath would be avoided.

Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth; exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ (16:3)

Allah, the Exalted, says, making known to His creation His proof against them regarding His oneness, and that divinity is fit for none but Him: "He created your Lord, O people, the heavens and the earth in justice, and that is the truth, alone in creating them, no partner having shared with Him in their origination and bringing into being, and no helper having aided Him in it. So how could He have a partner?" ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾: His majesty, may His praise be exalted, says: "Your Lord, O people, is high above your associating and your claim of a god besides Him. He is elevated above having any like, partner, or supporter, for none can be a god except one who creates and originates by His power the like of the heavens and the earth, and innovates bodies, bringing them into being from nothing. That is not within the power of anyone other than Allah, the One, the Subduer, to whom alone worship is due and for whom alone divinity is fit, and for nothing else."

**On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid, and behold, he is an open adversary﴾ (4)**

He, the Exalted, says: And among His proofs against you as well, O people, is that He created man from a drop of fluid. From a contemptible water He produced a wondrous creation. He turned him through stages, creation after creation, within three darknesses. Then He brought him forth into the light of the world after his creation was complete and the spirit had been breathed into him. He nourished him, provided him with sustenance, and made him grow. Then, when he had attained his full strength, he disbelieved in the blessing of his Lord, denied his Sustainer, worshipped one who neither harms nor benefits, and disputed with his God, saying ﴿Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?﴾ and forgetting the One who created him and perfected him into a sound form from a contemptible water. By "clear" (mubin) is meant that he expresses his disputation by his speech and argues with his tongue, and that is his clarity of expression. By "man" (insan) is meant all people; it is expressed in the singular, but it has the sense of the plural.

* *

**On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾ (5)**

He, the Exalted, says: And among His proofs against you, O people, is what He created for you of cattle, subjecting them to you. He made for you from their wool, their fur and their hair garments with which you keep warm, and benefits from their milk, and their backs which you ride. ﴿And from them you eat﴾ means: and of the cattle are those whose flesh you eat, such as camels, cattle and sheep, and all other animals whose flesh is eaten. The word "ma" has been omitted from the speech, since the meaning is indicated by "min" (from) before it.

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) said similar to what we have said regarding this.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verses 6–7:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back [to shelter] in the evening and when you send them out to graze in the morning. And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾

He, the Exalted, says: And for you in these livestock and cattle, which He created for you, is ﴿beauty when you bring them back﴾, meaning: when you drive them in the evening from their pasturing to their pen (al-mirah) and their dwellings where they take shelter. This is why the place is called al-mirah (the pen), because they are brought back to it in the evening and take shelter there. It is said of it: "Arah (so-and-so) brought back his livestock (araha mashiyatahu), so he brings them back (yurihuha) with bringing back (iraha)." As for His words ﴿and when you send them out to graze﴾, He says: and at the time when you bring them out in the morning from their pen to their pasture. It is said of it: "Sarah (so-and-so) sent out his livestock (sarraha mashiyatahu) to graze, sending them out (tasrihan), when he drives them out to pasture in the morning." And "sarahat al-mashiyah" means the livestock went out to pasture, going out (sarhan wa surhan). So al-sarh is in the morning, and al-iraha is in the evening. From this is the poet's saying:

"As if the remnants of the she-asses' traces upon his back were the tracks of the locusts (al-dabba) upon the sand-dune (al-naqa), while it is grazing (sarih)."

[Perhaps the poet describes a wild ass. He means that the she-asses have bitten him, leaving marks on his back which were like a path for locusts, the young locusts. "Upon the naqa," which is the white sand-hill. I have not found the verse nor its speaker.]

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said. Those who said this:

Bishr b. Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back and when you send them out﴾: "That is most wondrous when they come back with their udders swollen and their humps long, and when they are sent out to graze."

Muhammad b. Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad b. Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back and when you send them out﴾, he said: "When they come back they are at their greatest in humps and at their finest in udders."

* *

And His words ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾

He says: And these livestock carry your loads to another land which you would not have reached except with severe effort from yourselves and great toil.

As:

Ahmad b. Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Jabir, from Ikrimah, ﴿and they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "If you burdened yourselves with it, you would not reach it except with severe effort."

Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: Yahya b. Adam narrated to us, from Sharik, from Simak, from Ikrimah, ﴿to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "If you were to burden yourselves with it, you would not reach it except with great hardship."

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Simak, from Ikrimah, ﴿to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "The land: Makkah."

Muhammad b. Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa'; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, saying: Shibl narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, from Warqa', all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God ﴿except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "Hardship upon you."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he says: "With the toil of the souls (bijahd al-anfus)."

Muhammad b. Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad b. Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, the like of it.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of the regional centres recited it with a kasra on the shin: ﴿illa bi-shiqqi al-anfus﴾ (shiqq: hardship), except Abu Ja'far the reciter, for al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman b. Abi Hammad narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'id al-Razi narrated to me, from Abu Ja'far, reciter of Madinah, that he used to recite "lam takunu baligihi illa bi-shaqq al-anfus" with a fatha on the shin, and he would say: "The shaqq is only shaqq al-nafs (the hardship of the soul)." Ibn Abi Hammad said: Mu'adh al-Harra' used to say: "It is a dialect: the Arabs say bi-shaqq and bi-shiqq, and baraq and bi-riq."

The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is what the readers of the regional centres have, namely the kasra on the shin, due to the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it and the anomaly of what contradicts it. This verse is also recited with kasra and fatha of the shin, as in the poet's saying:

"And one who has camels, who strives for them and reckons them a burden, weary of their hardship and their toil."

[The verse is by al-Namir b. Tawlab al-Uklubi (Lisan: sh-q-q). Abu Ubaydah said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (1:356): "illa bi-shiqq al-anfus" with kasra and fatha of the first letter, its meaning: with hardship of the souls. In Lisan: al-shiqq is hardship. Ibn Bari said: the evidence for the kasra is the saying of al-Namir b. Tawlab: "And one who has camels..." the verse.]

Also "min shaqqiha" with kasra and fatha, and likewise the saying of al-Ajjaj:

"He became a camel-driver (maskhul) who confronts shaqqan..."

[The verse is in the Diwan of al-Ajjaj (Leipzig edition, 1903, p. 440), and it is evidence that al-shiqq with kasra means hardship. Maskhul: meaning his camel; yuwazi: meaning he endures.]

And "shaqqan" with fatha and kasra. By his saying "yuwazi shaqqan" he means: he endures hardship. Some grammarians of Arabic held that with fatha it is the verbal noun of shaqqa 'alayhi ashuqqu shaqqan, and with kasra it is the noun. It may be that those who recited with kasra intended: "except with a diminution of strength and the loss of part of it, so that one does not reach it except after its diminution; so its meaning then is: you would not have reached it except with the hardship of the strength of your souls and the loss of their other half." It is related from the Arabs: "Take this shiqq," meaning the portion of a sheep (shiqqat al-shah), with kasra. As for "shaqqat 'alayka shaqqan," only the accusative (nasb) has been recorded for it.

* *

And His words ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾

He, the Exalted, says: Indeed your Lord, O people, is full of compassion (ra'fah) for you and mercy, from His mercy upon you, He created the livestock for your benefits and your welfare, and He created the heavens and the earth as signs for you of the oneness of your Lord and the knowledge of your God, so that you may give thanks for His blessings upon you, and He will increase you from His bounty.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verses 6–7:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back [to shelter] in the evening and when you send them out to graze in the morning. And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾

He, the Exalted, says: And for you in these livestock and cattle, which He created for you, is ﴿beauty when you bring them back﴾, meaning: when you drive them in the evening from their pasturing to their pen (al-mirah) and their dwellings where they take shelter. This is why the place is called al-mirah (the pen), because they are brought back to it in the evening and take shelter there. It is said of it: "Arah (so-and-so) brought back his livestock (araha mashiyatahu), so he brings them back (yurihuha) with bringing back (iraha)." As for His words ﴿and when you send them out to graze﴾, He says: and at the time when you bring them out in the morning from their pen to their pasture. It is said of it: "Sarah (so-and-so) sent out his livestock (sarraha mashiyatahu) to graze, sending them out (tasrihan), when he drives them out to pasture in the morning." And "sarahat al-mashiyah" means the livestock went out to pasture, going out (sarhan wa surhan). So al-sarh is in the morning, and al-iraha is in the evening. From this is the poet's saying:

"As if the remnants of the she-asses' traces upon his back were the tracks of the locusts (al-dabba) upon the sand-dune (al-naqa), while it is grazing (sarih)."

[Perhaps the poet describes a wild ass. He means that the she-asses have bitten him, leaving marks on his back which were like a path for locusts, the young locusts. "Upon the naqa," which is the white sand-hill. I have not found the verse nor its speaker.]

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said. Those who said this:

Bishr b. Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back and when you send them out﴾: "That is most wondrous when they come back with their udders swollen and their humps long, and when they are sent out to graze."

Muhammad b. Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad b. Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back and when you send them out﴾, he said: "When they come back they are at their greatest in humps and at their finest in udders."

* *

And His words ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾

He says: And these livestock carry your loads to another land which you would not have reached except with severe effort from yourselves and great toil.

As:

Ahmad b. Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Jabir, from Ikrimah, ﴿and they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "If you burdened yourselves with it, you would not reach it except with severe effort."

Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: Yahya b. Adam narrated to us, from Sharik, from Simak, from Ikrimah, ﴿to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "If you were to burden yourselves with it, you would not reach it except with great hardship."

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Simak, from Ikrimah, ﴿to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "The land: Makkah."

Muhammad b. Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa'; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, saying: Shibl narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, from Warqa', all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God ﴿except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he said: "Hardship upon you."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, he says: "With the toil of the souls (bijahd al-anfus)."

Muhammad b. Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad b. Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, the like of it.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of the regional centres recited it with a kasra on the shin: ﴿illa bi-shiqqi al-anfus﴾ (shiqq: hardship), except Abu Ja'far the reciter, for al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman b. Abi Hammad narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'id al-Razi narrated to me, from Abu Ja'far, reciter of Madinah, that he used to recite "lam takunu baligihi illa bi-shaqq al-anfus" with a fatha on the shin, and he would say: "The shaqq is only shaqq al-nafs (the hardship of the soul)." Ibn Abi Hammad said: Mu'adh al-Harra' used to say: "It is a dialect: the Arabs say bi-shaqq and bi-shiqq, and baraq and bi-riq."

The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is what the readers of the regional centres have, namely the kasra on the shin, due to the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it and the anomaly of what contradicts it. This verse is also recited with kasra and fatha of the shin, as in the poet's saying:

"And one who has camels, who strives for them and reckons them a burden, weary of their hardship and their toil."

[The verse is by al-Namir b. Tawlab al-Uklubi (Lisan: sh-q-q). Abu Ubaydah said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (1:356): "illa bi-shiqq al-anfus" with kasra and fatha of the first letter, its meaning: with hardship of the souls. In Lisan: al-shiqq is hardship. Ibn Bari said: the evidence for the kasra is the saying of al-Namir b. Tawlab: "And one who has camels..." the verse.]

Also "min shaqqiha" with kasra and fatha, and likewise the saying of al-Ajjaj:

"He became a camel-driver (maskhul) who confronts shaqqan..."

[The verse is in the Diwan of al-Ajjaj (Leipzig edition, 1903, p. 440), and it is evidence that al-shiqq with kasra means hardship. Maskhul: meaning his camel; yuwazi: meaning he endures.]

And "shaqqan" with fatha and kasra. By his saying "yuwazi shaqqan" he means: he endures hardship. Some grammarians of Arabic held that with fatha it is the verbal noun of shaqqa 'alayhi ashuqqu shaqqan, and with kasra it is the noun. It may be that those who recited with kasra intended: "except with a diminution of strength and the loss of part of it, so that one does not reach it except after its diminution; so its meaning then is: you would not have reached it except with the hardship of the strength of your souls and the loss of their other half." It is related from the Arabs: "Take this shiqq," meaning the portion of a sheep (shiqqat al-shah), with kasra. As for "shaqqat 'alayka shaqqan," only the accusative (nasb) has been recorded for it.

* *

And His words ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾

He, the Exalted, says: Indeed your Lord, O people, is full of compassion (ra'fah) for you and mercy, from His mercy upon you, He created the livestock for your benefits and your welfare, and He created the heavens and the earth as signs for you of the oneness of your Lord and the knowledge of your God, so that you may give thanks for His blessings upon you, and He will increase you from His bounty.

On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [Qur'an 16:8]

He, the Exalted, says: And He created horses, mules and donkeys for you too, for riding and as adornment; that is: and made them for you as an adornment by which you adorn yourselves, along with the benefits they hold for you, such as riding and other things. The horses and mules are in the accusative case as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the pronoun in His words ﴿He created them﴾. The word "adornment" (zīnah) is in the accusative by a verb understood, as I have explained. Had there not been a waw with it and the sentence been "for you to ride them, an adornment," it would have been in the accusative by the verb preceding it, to which it is connected. But the presence of the waw indicates that there is an implied verb accompanying it, and that it is detached from the verb preceding it.

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding ﴿for you to ride and as adornment﴾: He made them for you to ride, and made them an adornment for you. Some of the people of knowledge held that in this verse there is an indication of the prohibition of eating the flesh of horses.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Wāḍiḥ related to us, saying: Abū Ḍamrah related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from a man, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride﴾, he said: These are for riding. ﴿And cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth﴾, he said: These are for eating.

Yaʿqūb related to us, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah related to us, saying: Hishām al-Dastuwāʾī related to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr related to us, from a client of Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAlqamah: that Ibn ʿAbbās used to dislike the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys, and he would say: God said ﴿And cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾, so these are for eating; ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride﴾, so these are for riding.

Ibn Wakīʿ related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Minhāl, from Saʿīd, from Ibn ʿAbbās: that he was asked about the flesh of horses, so he disliked it and recited this verse ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride﴾ ... the verse.

Aḥmad related to us, saying: Abū Aḥmad related to us, saying: Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ related to us, from Ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Minhāl ibn ʿAmr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās: that he was asked about the flesh of horses, and he said: Recite what comes before it: ﴿And cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat. And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾. So he made those for eating and these for riding.

Ibn Wakīʿ related to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abī Ghaniyyah related to us, from his father, from al-Ḥakam, regarding ﴿And cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾: so he made eating from them. Then he recited until he reached ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride﴾, and said: He did not make eating from them permissible for you. He said: al-Ḥakam used to say: Horses, mules and donkeys are forbidden in the Book of God.

Aḥmad related to us, saying: Abū Aḥmad related to us, saying: Ibn Abī Ghaniyyah related to us, from al-Ḥakam, who said: The flesh of horses is forbidden in the Book of God; then he recited ﴿And cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits﴾ ... up to His words ﴿for you to ride﴾.

Other people of knowledge, besides them, disagreed with them in this interpretation, holding that this does not indicate the prohibition of anything. They held that God, the Majestic and Praised, only acquainted His servants, through this verse and the rest of what is at the beginning of this surah, with His blessings upon them, and alerted them thereby to His proofs and His evidences of His oneness, and to the error of the act of those among the polytheists who associate others with Him.

Mention of some who saw no harm in eating horse meat:

Ibn Wakīʿ related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Shuʿbah, from Mughīrah, from Ibrāhīm, from al-Aswad: that he ate horse meat.

Ibn Wakīʿ related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Shuʿbah, from al-Ḥakam, from Ibrāhīm, from al-Aswad, similarly.

Aḥmad related to us, saying: Abū Aḥmad related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, from Manṣūr, from Ibrāhīm, who said: Our companions slaughtered a horse in the pasture and ate from it, and they saw no harm in it.

The correct position on this matter, in our view, is what was said by the second group. That is because if His words, the Exalted, ﴿for you to ride﴾ indicated that they are not suitable [for eating] since they are for riding and not for eating, then His words ﴿in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾ would indicate that they are not suitable since they are for eating and not for warmth. And the consensus of all that riding what He, the Exalted, mentioned as ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is permissible and lawful, not forbidden, is clear evidence that eating what He mentioned as ﴿for you to ride﴾ is permissible and lawful, not forbidden, except for what has been explicitly stated as forbidden or what has an indication of its prohibition from the Book or from revelation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). As for this verse, it does not make the eating of anything forbidden. The indication of the prohibition of the flesh of domestic donkeys has been established by His revelation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and [the prohibition regarding] mules by what we have explained in our book, the Book of Foods (Kitāb al-Aṭʿimah), sufficiently so that it need not be repeated in this place, since this place is not one of the places for clarifying the prohibition of that. We have only mentioned what we have mentioned to show that there is no basis for the view of those who cite this verse as evidence for the prohibition of horse meat.

Aḥmad related to us, saying: Abū Aḥmad related to us, saying: Isrāʾīl related to us, from ʿAbd al-Karīm, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Jābir, who said: We used to eat horse meat in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). I said: And mules? He said: As for mules, no.

* *

And His words ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾

He, the Exalted, says: And your Lord creates, along with these things He has mentioned to you, what you do not know, of what He has prepared in Paradise for its people and in the Fire for its people, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among them is that which deviates. And had He willed, He would have guided you all.﴾ (16:9)

He, exalted is His mention, says: Upon Allah, O people, is the clarification of the path of truth for you. So whoever is guided, it is for his own soul, and whoever goes astray, it is only against it that he goes astray. The sabil (way, path) is the road, and qasd (direction) of the road is the straight one with no crookedness in it, as the rajiz (the reciter of a rajaz verse) said:

"So he turned away from the course of the direct road" [The verse is evidence that al-tariq al-qasid means the straight one. In Lisan al-Arab: al-qasd is the straightness of the road; qasada yaqsudu qasdan, so he is qasid. As for His saying, "And upon Allah is the direction of the way" (i.e., upon Allah is the explanation of the straight path, and the calling with clear proofs and evidences), "and among them is that which deviates" means: and among them is a road that is not direct. And a qasid road is easy and straight.]

His saying ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾ means, exalted is His mention: and among the ways there is one that deviates from straightness and is crooked. So the qasid of the ways is Islam, and the jair (deviating) among them is Judaism, Christianity, and all the other creeds of disbelief, which deviate from the even way and its direction, apart from the upright monotheism of Islam. It has also been said: "among them" (minha, feminine), because sabil is feminine and may be masculine, so it was made feminine in this place. Some of them have said: it is said "minha" because sabil, although its wording is singular, its meaning is plural.

We have spoken in accordance with what the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Salih informed us, he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: he says: the clarification.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to us, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: he says: upon Allah is the clarification, that He clarify the guidance and the misguidance.

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us. And al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us. And al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, he said: Shibl narrated to us. And al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Ishaq informed us, he said: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, from Warqa', all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: he said: the path of truth is upon Allah.

- Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: he says: upon Allah is the clarification, the clarification of His lawful and unlawful, and of His obedience and disobedience.

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: he said: the sabil is the path of guidance.

- Ibn Wakit' narrated to us, he said: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: he said: its illumination.

- I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: he says: upon Allah is the clarification, He clarifies the guidance from the misguidance, and clarifies the ways that have diverged from His way, and among them is that which deviates.

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾: i.e., among the ways, the ways of Satan. And in the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "and among you is that which deviates, and had Allah willed, He would have guided you all."

- Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾: he said: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and among you is that which deviates."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾: he means: the scattered ways.

- 'Ali ibn Dawud narrated to me, he said: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾: he says: the divergent desires.

- I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾: he means the ways that have diverged from His way.

- Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾: the ways scattered from His way.

- Yunus narrated to us, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿and among them is that which deviates﴾: he said: among the ways there is one that deviates from the truth. He said: Allah said ﴿And do not follow the ways, lest they scatter you away from His way﴾ (6:153).

And His saying ﴿And had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾

He says: And had Allah willed, He would have shown kindness to all of you, O people, by His guidance, so you would have been guided and would have kept to the direct way, and would not have deviated from it, so that you would scatter into crooked ways away from the truth.

As:

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿And had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾: he said: Had He willed, He would have guided you all to the direct way, which is the truth. And he recited ﴿And had your Lord willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them together﴾ (10:99), the verse, and he recited ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ (32:13)... the verse.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 10:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿He it is who sends down water from the sky; from it is drink for you, and from it are trees in which you pasture [your animals]﴾

He, the Exalted, says: And the One who bestowed upon you these blessings, and created for you livestock, horses, and all other beasts for your benefit and welfare, is the Lord who sent down water from the sky, meaning rain, for you. From that water is drink which you drink, and from it [comes the water for] your trees and the life and growth of your plantings. ﴿In it you pasture﴾ means: in the trees that grow from the water sent down from the sky, you pasture, i.e., you graze [your livestock]. It is said from this: Aslama (to pasture) — "Fulan aslama his camels, yusimuhā, isāmah" — meaning he grazed them. Also, sawwamahā, yusawwimuhā, and they themselves sāmat, when they grazed; so they are sā'imah (grazing), and they are camels that are sā'imah (grazing freely). And from this it is said that livestock released into the wilderness or elsewhere to graze are called sā'imah. Some have related the meaning of sawm (pasturing) in sale to this, that each of the two parties to a transaction goes off in what suits him regarding an increase or decrease in price, just as grazing livestock go wherever they wish in their pastures. And from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"The people walked with the poles toward the pasture, and the one who pastured them was unable to find where the grazing was."[[The line is by al-A'sha ibn Tha'laba, Maymun ibn Qays (his Diwan, Cairo edition with the commentary of Dr. Muhammad Husayn, p. 213), from a qasida he composed in Najran yearning for his people and boasting of them. The narration in it reads "ilā al-Razḥā" instead of "ilā al-Mar'ā". He means: hunger weakened the camels, so they fell to the ground from exhaustion, and the people went to them, placing poles under their bellies to help them stand. "The one who pastured them" (a'yā al-musīm) was unable to find pasture because of the severity of the drought. Al-Razḥā: camels that become so emaciated they cannot walk and fall; it is the plural of rāzih. They place the poles under their bellies and then lift them. Al-Mīm is the active participle of āsama al-māshiyah: he pastured the livestock in the pasture. Abu 'Ubayda said in Majaz al-Qur'an (1: 357): it is said "asmat ibilī, wa sāmat hiya," meaning: I pastured them.]]

The interpreters have said something similar to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said that:

* Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from al-Nadr ibn 'Arabi, from 'Ikrimah, regarding ﴿And from it are trees in which you pasture﴾: he said, "you graze."

* Ahmad ibn Suhayl al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: Qurrah ibn 'Isa narrated to us, from al-Nadr ibn 'Arabi, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His saying ﴿in which you pasture﴾: he said, "you graze."

And the poet said:

"Like Ibn Bazi'a, or another like him — woe to you, son of the one who pastures the camels!"

He said: "O son of the shepherdess of camels!"

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verses 11–12:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the palm trees, the grapes, and of all the fruits. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾

His exalted remembrance says: Your Lord causes to grow for you, by means of the water which He sent down to you from the sky, your crops, your olives, your palm trees and your grapes. ﴿And of all the fruits﴾ means of all the other kinds of fruit, as provisions for you, sustenance, condiment and fruit, a blessing from Him upon you through that and a favour, and as a proof against those among you who disbelieve in Him. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ — He, may His praise be exalted, says: Indeed in God's bringing forth, by means of what He sends down from the sky of water, what He has described to you, there is ﴿a sign﴾, meaning a clear indication and a manifest mark. ﴿For a people who give thought﴾ means: for a people who take heed of God's admonitions and reflect upon His proofs, so that they remember and turn in repentance.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He made subservient to you the night and the day, the sun and the moon, and the stars are made subservient by His command. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason.﴾

His exalted remembrance says: And among His blessings upon you, O people, in addition to those He mentioned before, is that He made subservient to you the night and the day, alternating over you: the one for your going about in your livelihoods, and the other for your rest in it. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾ are for knowing the times of your seasons, your months and your years, and for the well-being of your livelihoods. ﴿And the stars are made subservient﴾ to you by God's command, running in their orbits so that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason﴾ — He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Indeed in God's subjecting those things to what He has subjected them to, there are clear proofs for a people who understand God's proofs and comprehend from Him His admonition to them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 13–14:

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿And whatever He has created for you on the earth, varied in its colours. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who remember﴾ (13).

Almighty God means by His saying ﴿And whatever He has created for you﴾, and subjected for you what He created: that is, what He created for you on the earth, varied in its colours, of animals and fruits.

As related:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And whatever He has created for you on the earth﴾: he said: "And what He created for you, varied in its colours, of animals, and of trees and fruits, blessings from God, abundant, so thank God for them."

- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: "Of animals, trees and fruits." The phrase "varied" (mukhtalifan) is in the accusative because His saying "whatever" (ma) is in the accusative position by the meaning I have described. Since that is so, "its colours varied" must be a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "ma", and the predicate is complete without it. Had "ma" not been in the accusative position, and the speech began with His saying "And whatever He has created for you," then "varied" could only be in the nominative, since it would then be the subject-complement of "ma".

* *

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh meat and extract from it ornaments that you wear. And you see the ships therein plowing [through], that you may seek of His bounty and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ (14).

Exalted is His remembrance, says: And He who did these deeds for you, and bestowed these blessings upon you, O people, is He who subjected the sea for you. The sea is every river, whether its water is salty or sweet. ﴿That you may eat from it fresh meat﴾, which is the fish that is hunted from it. ﴿And extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾, which are pearls and coral.

As related:

- Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Hisham informed us, from Amr, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh meat﴾: he said, "From both of them together." ﴿And extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾: he said, "This is pearls."

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, ﴿that you may eat from it fresh meat﴾: meaning the fish of the sea.

- Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Hammad related to us, from Yahya, saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Malik related to us, saying: A man came to Abu Ja'far and said: "Is there zakat on women's jewellery?" He said: "No. It is as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿ornaments that you wear, and you see the ships﴾," meaning the ships, ﴿plowing [through] therein﴾, and it is the plural of "makhirah".

The interpreters have differed regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿mawakhir﴾. Some of them said: "Mawakhir" means "laden" (mawaqir).

Those who said that:

- Amr ibn Musa al-Qazzaz related to us, saying: Abd al-Warith related to us, saying: Yunus related to us, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿And you see the ships plowing [through] therein﴾: he said, "Laden."

Others said regarding this what follows:

- Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Rabi'ah related to us, from Abu Bakr al-Asamm, from Ikrimah, regarding His saying ﴿And you see the ships plowing [through] therein﴾: he said, "What is taken from the water on the right and left of the ship is the mawakhir."

- Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Abu Makin, from Ikrimah, regarding His saying ﴿And you see the ships plowing [through] therein﴾: he said, "It is the ship that cuts through the water like this," meaning, it cleaves it.

Others said regarding it:

- Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: Abu Usamah related to us, from Isma'il, from Abu Salih, ﴿And you see the ships plowing [through] therein﴾: he said, "They run through it, cutting across."

Others said regarding it:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿And you see the ships plowing [through] therein﴾: he said, "The wind cleaves the ship, and the wind does not cleave ships except the great vessels."

- Al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, saying: Shibl related to us. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abd Allah related to us, from Warqa', all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly, except that al-Harith said in his report: "And the winds do not cleave the ships."

- Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, similarly.

- Yunus related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿mawakhir﴾: "It cleaves the wind."

Others said regarding it:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, ﴿And you see the ships plowing [through] therein﴾: "They run with one wind, coming and going."

- Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: "They run coming and going with one wind."

- Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, who said: "I heard al-Hasan," ﴿And you see the ships plowing [through] therein﴾: he said, "Coming and going with one wind." The "makhr" in the speech of the Arabs is the sound of the blowing of the wind when its blowing is strong, and in this place it is the sound of the ship's running with the wind when it is violent and the water cleaves its prow. It is said: "makharat al-safinah yamkhuru makhran wa makhuran, wa hiya makhirah." It is also said: "imtakhara al-rih" and "tamakhkharatuha," when one looks to see from where it blows and listens to the sound of its blowing. From this is the saying of Wasil, the client of Ibn Uyaynah: "It used to be said: If one of you wishes to urinate, let him test the wind (yatamakhkhar al-rih)," meaning by that: let him look from where its course and blowing come, so that he may turn his back to it, lest the urine return upon him and splash him.

* *

And His saying ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾.

Exalted is His remembrance, says: He subjected it for you so that you may dispose yourselves in seeking your livelihoods through trade.

As related:

- Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾: he said, "The trade of land and sea."

* *

And His saying ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾.

He says: So that you may thank your Lord for what He has bestowed upon you of these things, He subjected for you what He subjected of these things which He enumerated in these verses.

On the interpretation of His saying, ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with you, and rivers and roads, that you may be guided﴾ (16:15).

His saying, may He be exalted and remembered, means: and of His favours upon you, O people, is also that He cast into the earth firm mountains (rawasi), which is the plural of rasiyah, and these are the fixed mountains in the earth.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿lest it should shake with you﴾:

It means: lest it should not shake with you. This is like His saying, ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ (4:176), meaning: lest you go astray. The reason is that He, exalted is His praise, anchored the earth with mountains so that His creatures upon its surface would not be shaken, for it had been a swaying thing before it was anchored with them.

As related:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from Qays ibn 'Abbad: that when Allah, blessed and exalted, created the earth, it began to sway. The angels said: "This will not let anyone settle upon its back." So in the morning it had its mountains upon it.

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from 'Abd Allah ibn Habib, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: When Allah created the earth, it quaked and said: "My Lord, wilt Thou make upon me the children of Adam, who will work evil upon me and place filth upon me?" He said: "Then Allah set upon it mountains, what you see and what you do not see, and its settling became like flesh that quivers." Al-mayd is agitation and tilting. It is said: "The ship mada tamidu midan" when it tilts with its people and leans, and from it comes the mayd (seasickness) that afflicts the rider of the sea, which is dizziness.

The exegetes have said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿lest it should shake with you﴾: lest it should tilt with you.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying, ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with you﴾, he said: the mountains, lest it should shake with you. Qatadah said: I heard al-Hasan say: When the earth was created it nearly shook, so they said: "This will not let anyone settle upon its back." So in the morning the mountains had been created, and the angels did not know what the mountains had been created from.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and rivers﴾:

He says: and He placed in it rivers. So He conjoined the rivers to the mountains (rawasi), and gave them the same governing verb as the mountains, since the meaning and the intent of the speech was understood. This is like the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

You hear in their bellies a sawr (cry)... and in the two hands a hashshah and bawr.

[This is from rajaz verse, and I have not identified its speaker. Al-sawr means the sound (Lisan al-Arab), or it may be a corruption of al-dawr with a dad, meaning a sound resembling a moan in the belly from severe hunger. Lisan says: al-dawr is severe hunger, and al-tadawwur is writhing and crying out from the pain of a beating or hunger. Tadawwara the wolf, dog, lion, or fox: cried out from hunger. Al-hashshah, with a doubled shin, is dryness; it is said hasha the hand and ahasha, and he is mahush: it dried up. Most of this is said of paralysis. Al-bawr with a fatha is the verbal noun of bara, meaning perished and corrupted. Al-bawr also means a perished, corrupt person. Perhaps he intends to describe his she-camel as one harmed by hunger so that she cried out, and that in her hands there is dryness, i.e. paralysis and corruption. Imam al-Tabari has explained the point of evidence in the commentary.]

And the hashshah is dryness; so he conjoined the hashshah to the sound, and the hashshah is not heard, since the intended meaning was understood, and its meaning is: and you see in the two hands a hashshah.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and roads﴾:

It is the plural of sabil, just as turuq is the plural of tariq. The meaning of the speech is: and He placed for you, O people, on the earth, sabul and fijaj (open passages) which you traverse and in which you travel for your needs and the seeking of your livelihood, as a mercy to you and a favour from Him upon you in this. Had He blinded them to you, you would have perished in misguidance and bewilderment.

The exegetes have said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying, ﴿roads﴾: i.e. paths.

Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿roads﴾: he said: paths.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿that you may be guided﴾:

He says: so that you may be guided by these roads which He placed for you on the earth to the places you intend and the locations you desire, so that you do not go astray and become bewildered.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 16:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾ (16)

The scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the meaning of "landmarks." Some of them said: it means the signposts of the roads by day.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾: he meant by "landmarks" the signposts of the roads by day, and by "the star" they are guided by night.

Others said: it means the stars.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Yahya related to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, regarding ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾, he said: some of them are landmarks, and some of them are what they are guided by.

Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: my father related to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾, he said: some of them are a sign, and some of them are what one is guided by.

Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Qabisa related to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, the like of it.

Al-Muthanna said: "He said: Ishaq related to us," differing from Qabisa and Waki' in the chain of narration.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, his statement regarding ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾: "And the landmarks are the stars. Indeed Allah, blessed and exalted, created these stars for three purposes: He made them an adornment for the heaven, He made them something by which one is guided, and He made them missiles against the devils. Whoever occupies himself with other than that has erred in his opinion, missed his portion, wasted his share, and burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of."

Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿And landmarks﴾, he said: the stars.

Others said: it means the mountains.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Kalbi, regarding ﴿And landmarks﴾, he said: the mountains.

The most correct of these views, in our judgment, is to say: Allah, His remembrance is exalted, enumerated among His bounties upon His servants His favour to them in making for them landmarks by which they are guided on their paths and routes that they travel, and He did not specify some landmarks over others. Every sign by which people take guidance regarding their roads and the open paths of their ways falls under His words ﴿And landmarks﴾. "Paved roads" means those trodden, a sign of the intended direction; the mountains are landmarks by which one is guided to the aim of the way; and likewise the stars by night. However, what is more appropriate for the interpretation of the verse is that the landmarks are indications for the day, since Allah has separated out the indications of the night by His words ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾. When this is more fitting and more appropriate for the interpretation of the verse, it is necessary that the statement on this be what Ibn 'Abbas said in the report we narrated from 'Ata' from him, namely that the landmarks are the signposts of the roads and their markers by which one is guided to the straight course by day, and that the star by which one is guided by night is the Pole Star (al-Jaddi) and the two Fargadan, because by them travelers are guided rather than by other stars.

The meaning of the statement, then, is: And He placed for you, O people, landmarks by which you find your way by day on your journeys, and stars by which you are guided by night on your paths.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then take heed?﴾ (17) ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot number it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (18)

He, mentioned be His name, says to the worshippers of idols and images: Is He who creates these wondrous creatures that We have enumerated to you, and who bestows upon you these great blessings, like one who creates nothing and does not bestow upon you a single blessing, small or great? That is: Do you associate this with the worship of that? He makes them aware thereby of the magnitude of their ignorance, the badness of their view of themselves, and the scarcity of their gratitude to the One who bestowed upon them the blessings He has enumerated for them, which no one but Him can count. His Majesty, rebuking them, said to them: ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ O people, that is: will you not remember Allah's blessings upon you, His great authority and His power over whatever He wills, and the weakness, feebleness and abasement of your idols, and that they cannot bring to themselves any benefit nor ward off from themselves any harm, so that you may thereby recognize the error of what you persist in, of worshipping them and acknowledging them as divinities?

As reported:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then take heed?﴾: "Allah is the Creator, the Provider, while these idols that are worshipped besides Allah create nothing, and possess for their people neither harm nor benefit." Allah said: ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾

It has been said that ﴿one who creates not﴾ refers to the idol and the image, and that "man" (man) is used specifically for those endowed with discernment; but here it is used for other than them, for distinction, since it occurs as a differentiation between one who creates and one who does not create. It is related from the Arabs: "The rider and his camel became confused to me, so I did not know which is which," when the two were gathered together, and one of them is a human, and "man" was used appropriately for both of them. From this is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Of them is one that walks upon its belly, and of them is one that walks upon two legs, and of them is one that walks upon four﴾.

As for His words ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot number it﴾: you are not able to render the thanks due for it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: He, mentioned be His name, says: Indeed Allah is Forgiving of the shortcoming you have had in giving thanks for some of that, if you repent and turn back to His obedience and to pursuing His pleasure, and Merciful towards you, in not punishing you for it after you have turned to Him in repentance.

The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ [16:19] ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah create nothing, while they are created﴾ [16:20]

The Exalted says: And Allah, who is your God, O people, knows what you hide within yourselves of your inner thoughts, which you conceal from others, and what you show with your tongues and your limbs, and what you make public with your tongues, your limbs and your deeds. He takes account of all of it against you, so that He may recompense you for it on the Day of Resurrection: the one who does good among you with his good, and the one who does evil among you with his evil. And He will call you to account for what there was of your gratitude in this world for His blessings which He bestowed upon you therein, those which you counted and those which you could not count.

As for His words, ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah create nothing, while they are created﴾, the Exalted says: And your idols, which you call upon besides Allah, O people, as gods, create nothing, while they themselves are created. How can something be a god when it is made and managed, possessing no power to benefit or harm itself?

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verses 21–22:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ (21)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, to these polytheists of Quraysh: "And those whom you invoke besides Allah, O people," ﴿they are dead, not alive﴾. He, may His praise be exalted, described them as dead, not alive, since there are no spirits in them.

As [it is related]:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾: "These are the idols that are worshipped besides Allah. They are dead, with no spirits in them, and they cannot bring harm or benefit to their worshippers." Regarding the nominative case of "dead" there are two views: one is that it is the predicate of "those" (alladhina), and the other is that it is a new independent sentence. His saying ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ means: your idols, which you invoke besides Allah, do not know when they will be resurrected. It has also been said that this refers to the disbelievers, that they do not know when they will be resurrected.

* * *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Your God is one God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant﴾ (22)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: your object of worship, who deserves to be worshipped by you, and the singling out of obedience to Him apart from all other things, is one object of worship, because worship is fit only for Him. So single out obedience to Him, devote worship to Him exclusively, and do not set up any partner with Him. ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying﴾: His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, means: those who do not affirm the promise and threat of Allah, and do not acknowledge the return to Him after death, their hearts are denying, meaning they deny what has been recounted to them of Allah's power and greatness, and His beautiful blessings upon them, and that worship is fit only for Him, and that divinity belongs to nothing other than Him. He says: "And they are arrogant" toward singling out Allah with divinity and affirming His oneness, following what their forefathers had continued in of associating others with Allah.

As [it is related]:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying﴾: "[They deny] this account that has already passed, and they are arrogant toward it."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 23–24:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Without doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾ (23)

By His words, may He be exalted and remembered, "Without doubt" (la jarama), meaning truly, "Allah knows what these polytheists conceal of their denial of the reports we have mentioned in this surah, and their rejection of our saying to them, 'Your God is one God,' and their arrogance towards Allah, and what they reveal of their disbelief in Allah and their slander against Him." ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant﴾ means: Allah does not love those who are arrogant towards Him by refusing to declare Him one and by casting off what is worshipped besides Him of gods and rivals.

As related to us:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Awn narrated to us, saying: Mis'ar narrated to us, from a man: that al-Hasan ibn Ali used to sit with the poor, then he would say, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ (24)

His, may He be exalted and remembered, saying: When it is said to these polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter, "What has your Lord sent down?" meaning, "What thing has your Lord sent down?" they say: "What was sent down is what the ancients before us wrote down of falsehoods."

As for that:

As related to us:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Tales of the ancients"﴾, he said: "The stories of the ancients and their falsehoods." Some of the polytheists of the Arabs who used to sit on the road of those who came to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said this; when any of the believers passed by them, intending the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ), they would say to them, "Tales of the ancients," meaning: the stories of the ancients and their falsehoods.

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Tales of the ancients﴾, he said: "The stories of the ancients."
