Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 25:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and also some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably evil is that which they bear.﴾

His, the Exalted's, statement means: These polytheists say to whoever asks them, "What has your Lord sent down?", (the one) that our Lord has sent down, according to what Muhammad claims, (is) "the tales of the ancients", so that they may have their sins, in which they remain, arising from their denial of God and their disbelief in what was sent down to His Messenger (ﷺ), and some of the sins of those who turn them away from belief in God, who lead astray, who tempt some of them, without knowledge. His statement ﴿Unquestionably evil is that which they bear﴾ means: Unquestionably evil is the sin they commit and the burden they carry.

Similar to what we have said on this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His statement ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾: "And of the burdens of those they misled" means their bearing the sins of themselves and the sins of those who obeyed them, and that does not lessen the punishment for those who obeyed them in any way.

Al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similar to it, except that he said: "And of the burdens of those who mislead them" is their bearing the sins of themselves, and the rest of the report is similar.

Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: 'Abd Allah related to us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and also some of the burdens of those whom they mislead﴾, he said: "Their bearing their own sins and the sins of those who obeyed them, and that does not lessen the punishment for those who obeyed them in any way."

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, similar to it.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾, i.e., their sins and the sins of those they mislead without knowledge, ﴿Unquestionably evil is that which they bear﴾.

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His statement ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and also some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾: he said: they bear their sins, like His statement ﴿and burdens along with their own burdens﴾, meaning they bear, along with their sins, those whom they mislead without knowledge.

Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and also some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably evil is that which they bear﴾, he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever calls to misguidance and is followed, he has the like of the sins of those who follow him, without any diminution of their sins whatsoever. And whoever calls to guidance and is followed, he has the like of the rewards of those who follow him, without any diminution of their rewards whatsoever."

Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd informed us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from a man, who said: Zayd ibn Aslam said: "It reached him that a disbeliever's deed will take the form of the ugliest of God's creations in face and the most foul-smelling of scent. It sits beside him, and whenever something frightens him, it increases his fright, and whenever he fears something, it increases his fear. He says: 'What an evil companion you are! Who are you?' It says: 'Do you not know me?' He says: 'No.' It says: 'I am your deed, which was ugly, and that is why you see me ugly; it was foul, and that is why you see me foul. Lower yourself to me so I can ride you, for you rode me often in the world.' So he mounts it." This is His statement ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those before them had already plotted, but Allah came at their structures from the foundations, and the roof fell down on them from above them, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ (16:26)

He, dhikruhu, says: Those who came before these polytheists, who bar others from the way of Allah and from following the religion of Allah, had already plotted and sought to overpower Allah by building a structure, intending, by their claim, to rise up to the heaven to wage war against whoever is in it. The one who undertook this, as has been reported to us, was a tyrant from among the tyrants of the Nabateans. Some of them said he was Nimrod son of Canaan, and some said he was Nebuchadnezzar (Bukhtansar). Some of their reports have been mentioned in Surat Ibrahim. It has also been said that the one mentioned in this passage is the same one whom Allah mentions in Surat Ibrahim.

Those who said that:

Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: The one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord ordered that Ibrahim be expelled, meaning from his city. He met Lut at the gate of the city, and he was his nephew, so he called him, and he believed in him, and he said: "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord." Nimrod swore that he would seek the God of Ibrahim. So he took four chicks of vultures, raised them on meat and bread until they grew large, strong and sturdy, tied them to a chest, sat in that chest, and then raised a piece of meat for them, and they flew. When they had gone up into the sky, he looked down at the earth and saw the mountains crawling like ants. Then he raised the meat for them again, and looked, and saw the earth surrounded by a sea, as if it were a disc in water. Then he rose a long way and fell into darkness, so that he could see neither what was above him nor what was below him. He became frightened and threw down the meat, and they swooped after it. When the mountains saw them, as they came swooping and their rustling was heard, the mountains were terrified and nearly moved from their places, but they did not. That is the saying of Allah, exalted: ﴿And they had plotted their plot, but with Allah is their plot, though their plot was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾ (14:46). In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "And the plot of them was nearly..." (wa in kada makruhum). Their flight with him was from Jerusalem, and their landing with him was at Mount al-Dukhan. When he saw that he could not overcome anything, he set about building the tower. He built it until, when he had raised it to the sky, he climbed on top of it to look, claiming to see the God of Ibrahim. Then he defecated, though he had not been defecating before. Allah took its building from the foundations: ﴿So the roof fell down on them from above them, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾. He says: from their place of safety; He seized them from the base of the tower, so it collapsed upon them and fell down. The tongues of the people were confused that day from fear, and they spoke seventy-three languages, and for that reason it was named Babel. Previously the language of the people had been Syriac.

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Those before them had already plotted, but Allah came at their structures from the foundations﴾: He said: It is Nimrod, when he built the tower.

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Zayd ibn Aslam: The first tyrant on earth was Nimrod. Allah sent a gnat against him, which entered his nostril, and he remained for four hundred years being struck on the head with hammers, the most merciful of people toward him being the one who joined his hands and struck his head with them. He was a tyrant for four hundred years, and Allah punished him for four hundred years in proportion to his kingdom, then Allah caused him to die. He was the one who built the tower toward the sky, and he is the one of whom Allah said: ﴿So Allah came at their structures from the foundations, and the roof fell down on them from above them﴾. As for His saying ﴿Allah came at their structures from the foundations﴾, its meaning is: Allah demolished their building from its root. The "foundations" (al-qawa'id) is the plural of qa'idah, which is the base. Some of them used to say: this is an image for total uprooting, and its meaning is only that Allah uprooted them. He said: The Arabs say that when a thing is uprooted.

* *

As for His saying ﴿And the roof fell down on them from above them﴾:

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of that. Some of them said: its meaning is: the roof fell down on them from above them, that is, the upper parts of their houses from above them.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Those before them had already plotted, but Allah came at their structures from the foundations﴾: Indeed, by Allah, the decree of Allah came upon it from its base. ﴿And the roof fell down on them from above them﴾: the roof is the upper parts of the houses. Their houses were overturned upon them, and Allah destroyed and annihilated them. ﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿So the roof fell down on them from above them﴾, he said: Allah came at their structures from their roots, so the roof fell down on them.

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, saying: Shibl narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, from Warqa', all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Allah came at their structures from the foundations﴾, he said: The plot of Nimrod ibn Canaan, who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the same.

Others said: by His saying ﴿the roof fell down on them from above them﴾ He meant that the punishment came upon them from the sky.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿So the roof fell down on them from above them﴾: He says: a punishment from the sky; when they saw it, they submitted and were humbled.

The more correct of the two interpretations of the verse, in our view, is the saying of those who said: the meaning is that the roofs of their houses fell down upon them, when the decree of Allah came upon their roots and foundations, so their dwellings were overturned upon them, because that is the familiar meaning of the foundations of a building, and "the roof fell down" is the common usage; directing the meanings of the words of Allah to their most well-known and recognized sense is more appropriate than directing them to other meanings for which no sound basis exists.

﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾. He, dhikruhu, says: And the punishment of Allah came upon those who plotted before them, the polytheists of Quraysh, from where they did not know that it had come to them from it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 27:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners, about whom you used to dispute?" Those who were given knowledge will say, "Indeed, disgrace this Day and evil are upon the disbelievers."﴾ (16:27)

The Exalted says: As for what Allah did to those who schemed, whose affair Allah, glorified is His praise, has described, of what He did to them in this world, by hastening punishment upon them and exacting retribution for their disbelief and their denial of His oneness, then, in addition to that, on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them, humiliating them with a painful punishment, and will say to them when they come before Him, ﴿Where are My partners about whom you used to dispute?﴾ Its origin: "I opposed (shaqqaqtu) so-and-so, and he opposes (yushaqqqunī) me," which is when each of the two does to the other what is hard for him to bear. The Exalted says, on the Day of Resurrection, rebuking the polytheists for their worship of idols: "Where are My partners?" That is, where are those whom you claimed in the world to be My partners today? Why do they not attend you, so that they might repel from you the punishment with which I am about to visit you? For you used to worship them in the world and take them as allies, and an ally supports his ally. Their disputing with Allah regarding their idols was their opposing Him in their worship.

As for what has been narrated:

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Where are My partners about whom you used to dispute?﴾ He said: "You used to oppose Me."

* *

And His saying ﴿Indeed, disgrace this Day and evil are upon the disbelievers.﴾

Meaning: the abasement, humiliation and evil, that is, the punishment of Allah upon the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 28:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: Those who were given knowledge said: Indeed, disgrace today and evil are upon those who disbelieved in God, denying His oneness. ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾ means: those whose souls the angels seize. ﴿While they are wronging themselves﴾ means: while they are upon their disbelief and their associating others with God. It was also said that by this He meant those of Quraysh who were killed at Badr, who were taken out to it against their will.

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Ya'qub ibn Muhammad al-Zuhri told us, saying: Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna told me, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ikrimah, who said: There were people in Mecca who professed Islam but did not emigrate, so they were taken out against their will to Badr, and some of them were killed. So God revealed concerning them: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾

And His words: ﴿So they will offer submission﴾

He means: they submitted to His command and yielded to Him when they witnessed death had come down upon them. ﴿We did not used to do any evil﴾. In the speech there is an omitted element, the hearers' understanding of which is sufficient without mention, what the speech indicates, namely: they said, "We did not used to do any evil." He reports about them that they lied and said: "We did not used to disobey God," holding fast to falsehood in hope that they would be saved by it. So God refuted them and said: ﴿Rather, you used to do evil and bar from the way of God﴾. ﴿Indeed, God is Knowing of what you used to do﴾ means: indeed God has knowledge of what you used to do in the world of His disobedience, and what you committed in it that angers Him.

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, Words: "So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein. Wretched is the abode of the arrogant." (29)

He, the Exalted, says, saying to these wrongdoers themselves when they say to their Lord, "We did not do any evil": "Enter the gates of Hell," meaning: its levels (tabaqat), "to abide therein," meaning: remaining in it, "Wretched is the abode of the arrogant," meaning: wretched is the dwelling place of those who were arrogant toward God, did not acknowledge His lordship, and did not affirm His oneness, which is Hell.

* *

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, Words: "And it will be said to those who were God-fearing, 'What has your Lord sent down?' They will say, 'Good.' For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing." (30)

He, the Exalted, says: It will be said to the other group, those who are people of faith and piety toward God, "What has your Lord sent down?" "They say, 'Good.'" That is: they say, "He sent down good." Some of the grammarians of Kufa used to say: the Bedouins (al-a'rab) differed only in His words "They say, 'Tales of the ancients'" and His words "Good," whereas the matter before both answers is one and the same, namely His words "What has your Lord sent down?" Because the disbelievers denied the revelation, so when they heard it they said, "Tales of the ancients," meaning: what you have brought is the tales of the ancients, and God has sent down nothing of it. As for the believers, they affirmed the revelation, so they said "Good," meaning that He sent down good. Thus it is accusative (intasaba) by the verb's falling from God upon the good, and this is why the two differ. Then he began the report, saying: "For those who did good in this world there is good." We have already explained the discussion on this earlier, in a manner that suffices without repeating it.

* *

As for His words: "For those who did good in this world there is good,"

He, the Exalted, says: for those who believed in God in this world and in His Messenger, and obeyed Him therein, and called the servants of God to faith and to acting by what God commanded, "good" means: honor from God. "And the abode of the Hereafter is better," meaning: the abode of the Hereafter is better for them than the abode of this world, and the honor of God which He has prepared for them there is greater than the honor which He hastened to them in this world. "And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing," meaning: excellent is the abode of the Hereafter for those who feared God in this world, guarding against His punishment by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions.

Concerning this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: "And it will be said to those who were God-fearing, 'What has your Lord sent down?' They will say, 'Good. For those who did good in this world there is good.'" He said: These are believers; it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" and they say, "Good. For those who did good in this world there is good," meaning: they believed in God, were commanded to obey God, urged the people of God's obedience to good, and called them to it.

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, Words: "So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein. Wretched is the abode of the arrogant." (29)

He, the Exalted, says, saying to these wrongdoers themselves when they say to their Lord, "We did not do any evil": "Enter the gates of Hell," meaning: its levels (tabaqat), "to abide therein," meaning: remaining in it, "Wretched is the abode of the arrogant," meaning: wretched is the dwelling place of those who were arrogant toward God, did not acknowledge His lordship, and did not affirm His oneness, which is Hell.

* *

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, Words: "And it will be said to those who were God-fearing, 'What has your Lord sent down?' They will say, 'Good.' For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing." (30)

He, the Exalted, says: It will be said to the other group, those who are people of faith and piety toward God, "What has your Lord sent down?" "They say, 'Good.'" That is: they say, "He sent down good." We have already explained the discussion on this earlier, in a manner that suffices without repeating it.

* *

As for His words: "For those who did good in this world there is good,"

He, the Exalted, says: for those who believed in God in this world and in His Messenger, and obeyed Him therein, and called the servants of God to faith and to acting by what God commanded, "good" means: honor from God. "And the abode of the Hereafter is better," meaning: the abode of the Hereafter is better for them than the abode of this world, and the honor of God which He has prepared for them there is greater than the honor which He hastened to them in this world. "And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing," meaning: excellent is the abode of the Hereafter for those who feared God in this world, guarding against His punishment by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions.

Concerning this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: "And it will be said to those who were God-fearing, 'What has your Lord sent down?' They will say, 'Good. For those who did good in this world there is good.'" He said: These are believers; it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" and they say, "Good. For those who did good in this world there is good," meaning: they believed in God, were commanded to obey God, urged the people of God's obedience to good, and called them to it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 31:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Gardens of Eden, they will enter them, beneath which rivers flow; for them therein is whatever they wish. Thus does Allah reward the God-fearing﴾

He, the Exalted, means by His words ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾: gardens of abiding (al-maqam). We have already explained the differences of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) regarding the meaning of "Eden" earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. ﴿They will enter them﴾ means: they will enter the Gardens of Eden. As for the case of ﴿jannatu﴾ (gardens) in the nominative, there are three possibilities. The first: that it is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). The second: that it is nominative by the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) in the mention in His words ﴿they will enter them﴾. The third: that it is the predicate (khabar) of "ni'ma" (what an excellent...), so that the meaning, when you take it as the predicate of ni'ma, is: "And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing: Gardens of Eden." In this case ﴿they will enter them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as one says: "Excellent is the abode, an abode you dwell in." It is also permissible, when the sentence is given this interpretation, that ﴿they will enter them﴾ be a relative clause (silah) of ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾.

His words ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ mean: rivers flow beneath its trees. ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾ means: for those who did good in this world, in the Gardens of Eden is whatever they wish of what their souls desire and their eyes delight in. ﴿Thus does Allah reward the God-fearing﴾ means: just as Allah rewards those who did good in this world with what He has described to you, O people, as their reward in this world and the Hereafter, so too He rewards those who fear Him by performing His obligations and avoiding His disobediences.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 32:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His mention: ﴿Those whose souls the angels take while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter Paradise for what you used to do."﴾

He, exalted is His mention, says: Thus does Allah reward the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), those whose souls the angels of Allah seize, and they are good by Allah's making them good, through the purity of faith and the cleanness of Islam during their life and at their death.

As:

* Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid. And al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us. And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa informed us, saying: Shibl narrated to us. And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, from Warqa, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿those whose souls the angels take while they are good﴾, he said: "Living and dead; Allah decreed that for them."

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

And His saying ﴿saying, "Peace be upon you"﴾

He, exalted is His mention, means that the angels take the souls of these God-fearing people, and they say to them: "Peace be upon you; proceed to Paradise," as glad tidings from Allah which the angels convey to them.

As:

* Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Abu Sakhr informed me, that he heard Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi say: "When the soul of the believing servant is about to depart, an angel comes to him and says: 'Peace be upon you, friend of Allah; Allah sends you His greetings.'" Then he recited this verse ﴿those whose souls the angels take while they are good﴾ ... to the end of the verse.

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata al-Khurasani, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Peace be upon you from the companions of the right hand﴾, he said: "The angels come to him with greetings from Allah, and inform him that he is one of the companions of the right hand."

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: al-Ashabb Abu Ali narrated to us, from Abu Raja, from Muhammad ibn Malik, from al-Bara, who said regarding His saying ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾: "He greets him at the time of death."

* *

And His saying ﴿for what you used to do﴾

He says: for what you used to strive after in the world during your lifetimes there, seeking obedience to Allah and the pursuit of His good pleasure.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 33:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they await only that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come? Thus did those before them act. And Allah did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

His saying, exalted is His remembrance: Do these polytheists await only that the angels come to them to seize their souls, or that the command of your Lord come, that is, that they be gathered to the station of the Resurrection? ﴿Thus did those before them act.﴾ He, may His praise be exalted, says: just as these people wait for the angels of Allah to seize their souls, or for the coming of the command of Allah, so did their predecessors among the disbelievers in Allah act, for that applies to every polytheist who associates others with Allah. ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾ He, may His praise be exalted, says: and Allah did not wrong them by bringing down His wrath upon them, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ by their disobedience to their Lord and their disbelief in Him, until they deserved His punishment, so He hastened it upon them.

And the scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying, ﴿Do they await only that the angels should come to them﴾: "With death." And in another verse He said: ﴿If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve﴾, and he is the Angel of Death, and he has messengers. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿or that the command of your Lord should come﴾: that is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Do they await only that the angels should come to them﴾: he said: "At the time of death, when they take their souls. Or that the command of your Lord should come": that is the Day of Resurrection.

The discussion of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them, and what they had been mocking encompassed them﴾ (16:34).

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: So there befell those of the earlier nations who did as these polytheists of Quraysh are doing the evil consequences of what they had done, meaning the punishments for their sins and the vengeance for their disobediences which they had earned. ﴿And what they had been mocking encompassed them﴾ means: there descended upon them from the punishment of God that which they had been mocking and deriding when the messengers of God warned them of it, and it befell them specifically and not others among the people of faith in God.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who associated others with God said: "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything without Him."﴾ So did those before them do. So is there upon the messengers aught but clear conveyance?﴾

The exalted One says: Those who associated others with God, worshipping idols and images besides God, said: "We do not worship these images except because God has approved of our worshipping them. Nor do we forbid what we have forbidden, such as the baheera and the sawaiba, except that God willed this prohibition from us and from our fathers, and was pleased with it. Had God not willed it, He would have changed it by some of His punishments, or by guiding us away from it to other deeds."

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Thus did those before them act, those polytheistic nations whose way these people followed. They said the same as what these people said, and they took the same path in denying the messengers of God and in following the deeds of their fathers in error.

As for His saying ﴿So is there upon the messengers aught but clear conveyance?﴾, the exalted One says: So then, O you who say "Had God willed, we would not have associated anything, nor would our fathers," is there upon Our messengers, whom We send to warn you of Our punishment for your disbelief, anything but clear conveyance? That is: nothing but that they convey to you what We have sent to you of the message. By His saying "the clear" (al-mubin) He means: the one who makes its meaning clear to whoever is conveyed to, so that the one to whom it is sent understands it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 36–37:

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying]: "Worship Allah and avoid al-Taghut (false deities)." Then among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ (16:36)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And We certainly sent, O people, into every nation that passed before you a messenger, just as We sent [one] among you, [commanding them] that they worship Allah alone, without partner, and devote obedience to Him and sincerely dedicate worship to Him. ﴿And avoid al-Taghut﴾ means: keep far from Satan, and beware lest he lead you astray and turn you away from the way of Allah, so that you go astray. ﴿Then among them were those whom Allah guided﴾ means: among those to whom We sent Our messengers, there were those whom Allah guided, granting them success to confirm His messengers, to accept from them, to believe in Allah, and to act in obedience to Him; so they prospered, attained success, and were saved from the punishment of Allah. ﴿And among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ means: and among the nations to whom We sent Our messengers, there were others upon whom error was justly decreed, so they deviated from the straight way, disbelieved in Allah, denied His messengers, and followed al-Taghut; so Allah destroyed them with His punishment and sent down upon them His might, which is not turned back from the criminal people. ﴿So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ means: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to the polytheists of Quraysh: If you, O people, do not affirm Our messenger concerning what he tells you of these nations upon whom there befell what befell of Our might because of their disbelief in Allah and their denial of His messenger, then travel through the land they used to inhabit and the towns they used to populate, and look at the traces of Allah among them and the traces of His wrath descending upon them, and how their denial of the messengers of Allah brought upon them what it brought. For you will see the reality of that, and by it you will know the truth of the report that Muhammad (ﷺ) tells you.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those who lead themselves astray, and for them there are no helpers.﴾ (16:37)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): If you, O Muhammad, are eager for the guidance of these polytheists to belief in Allah and following the truth, ﴿then indeed Allah does not guide those who lead themselves astray﴾.

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the Kufan reciters read ﴿fa-inna Allaha la yahdi man yudill﴾ with a fatha on the yā' of yahdi and a ḍamma on the yā' of yudill. The grammarians of Kufa differed concerning the meaning of this reading. Some of the grammarians of Kufa claimed that its meaning is: indeed, whomever Allah misguides does not become guided, and he said: the Arabs say "qad hadā al-rajul," meaning "qad ihtadā" (he has been guided), and hadā and ihtadā have one meaning. Others among them claimed that its meaning is: indeed Allah does not guide whomever He misguides, meaning: whomever Allah misguides, Allah does not guide him. The majority of the reciters of Medina, Syria and Basra read ﴿fa-inna Allaha la yuhdā﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā' of yuhdā and of yuḍill, and a fatha on the dāl of yuhdā, meaning: whomever Allah misguides, there is no guide for him.

This reading is, in my view, the more correct of the two readings, because yahdi in the sense of yahtadi is rare and not widespread in the speech of the Arabs, and because there is no benefit in the saying of one who says: whomever Allah misguides, He does not guide him, since that is something no one is ignorant of. And since that is so, a reading in accordance with what is widespread in the language of the Arabs, which carries great benefit, is more fitting and more deserving.

So the interpretation of the speech, if the matter is as we have described, is: If you, O Muhammad, are eager for their guidance, then whomever Allah misguides has no guide, so do not exert yourself over his affair, but convey to him what you were sent with, so that the proof may be established against him. ﴿And for them there are no helpers﴾ means: and for them there is no helper who will help them against Allah if He wills to punish them, so that he might prevent between Allah and what He wills of their punishment.

Regarding His words ﴿in taḥraṣ﴾ there are two dialects. Among the Arabs there are those who say ḥaraṣa, yaḥraṣu, with a fatḥa on the rā' in the past form and a kasra in the present form, and ḥariṣa, yaḥraṣu, with a kasra on the rā' in the past form and a fatḥa in the present form. The reading is with fatḥa in the past and kasra in the present, and this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 36–37:

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying]: "Worship Allah and avoid al-Taghut (false deities)." Then among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ (16:36)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And We certainly sent, O people, into every nation that passed before you a messenger, just as We sent [one] among you, [commanding them] that they worship Allah alone, without partner, and devote obedience to Him and sincerely dedicate worship to Him. ﴿And avoid al-Taghut﴾ means: keep far from Satan, and beware lest he lead you astray and turn you away from the way of Allah, so that you go astray. ﴿Then among them were those whom Allah guided﴾ means: among those to whom We sent Our messengers, there were those whom Allah guided, granting them success to confirm His messengers, to accept from them, to believe in Allah, and to act in obedience to Him; so they prospered, attained success, and were saved from the punishment of Allah. ﴿And among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ means: and among the nations to whom We sent Our messengers, there were others upon whom error was justly decreed, so they deviated from the straight way, disbelieved in Allah, denied His messengers, and followed al-Taghut; so Allah destroyed them with His punishment and sent down upon them His might, which is not turned back from the criminal people. ﴿So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ means: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to the polytheists of Quraysh: If you, O people, do not affirm Our messenger concerning what he tells you of these nations upon whom there befell what befell of Our might because of their disbelief in Allah and their denial of His messenger, then travel through the land they used to inhabit and the towns they used to populate, and look at the traces of Allah among them and the traces of His wrath descending upon them, and how their denial of the messengers of Allah brought upon them what it brought. For you will see the reality of that, and by it you will know the truth of the report that Muhammad (ﷺ) tells you.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those who lead themselves astray, and for them there are no helpers.﴾ (16:37)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): If you, O Muhammad, are eager for the guidance of these polytheists to belief in Allah and following the truth, ﴿then indeed Allah does not guide those who lead themselves astray﴾.

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the Kufan reciters read ﴿fa-inna Allaha la yahdi man yudill﴾ with a fatha on the yā' of yahdi and a ḍamma on the yā' of yudill. The grammarians of Kufa differed concerning the meaning of this reading. Some of the grammarians of Kufa claimed that its meaning is: indeed, whomever Allah misguides does not become guided, and he said: the Arabs say "qad hadā al-rajul," meaning "qad ihtadā" (he has been guided), and hadā and ihtadā have one meaning. Others among them claimed that its meaning is: indeed Allah does not guide whomever He misguides, meaning: whomever Allah misguides, Allah does not guide him. The majority of the reciters of Medina, Syria and Basra read ﴿fa-inna Allaha la yuhdā﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā' of yuhdā and of yuḍill, and a fatha on the dāl of yuhdā, meaning: whomever Allah misguides, there is no guide for him.

This reading is, in my view, the more correct of the two readings, because yahdi in the sense of yahtadi is rare and not widespread in the speech of the Arabs, and because there is no benefit in the saying of one who says: whomever Allah misguides, He does not guide him, since that is something no one is ignorant of. And since that is so, a reading in accordance with what is widespread in the language of the Arabs, which carries great benefit, is more fitting and more deserving.

So the interpretation of the speech, if the matter is as we have described, is: If you, O Muhammad, are eager for their guidance, then whomever Allah misguides has no guide, so do not exert yourself over his affair, but convey to him what you were sent with, so that the proof may be established against him. ﴿And for them there are no helpers﴾ means: and for them there is no helper who will help them against Allah if He wills to punish them, so that he might prevent between Allah and what He wills of their punishment.

Regarding His words ﴿in taḥraṣ﴾ there are two dialects. Among the Arabs there are those who say ḥaraṣa, yaḥraṣu, with a fatḥa on the rā' in the past form and a kasra in the present form, and ḥariṣa, yaḥraṣu, with a kasra on the rā' in the past form and a fatḥa in the present form. The reading is with fatḥa in the past and kasra in the present, and this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 38:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die. Yes indeed! It is a promise binding upon Him, the truth, but most people do not know﴾.

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: These polytheists of Quraysh swore by God with their most emphatic oaths, their oath that God would not raise up those who die after their death. They lied and were mistaken in the oaths they swore thereby. Rather, God will indeed raise them after their death, a promise binding upon Him to raise them, the promise He made to His servants, and God does not break His promise. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ means: but most of Quraysh do not know God's promise to His servants, that He will raise them on the Day of Resurrection after their death, alive.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said concerning this.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, on the authority of Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die﴾: as a denial of God's command or of our command, for people became two groups regarding the resurrection: one denying and one affirming. It was related to us that a man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Some people in this Iraq claim that 'Ali will be raised before the Day of Resurrection, and they interpret this verse." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Those people lie. This verse is for people in general. By my life, if 'Ali were raised before the Day of Resurrection, we would not have married his wives, nor divided his inheritance."

Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, on the authority of Ma'mar, on the authority of Qatadah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed some men say that 'Ali will be raised before the Day of Resurrection, and they interpret ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die. Yes indeed! It is a promise binding upon Him, the truth, but most people do not know﴾." He said: "If we knew that 'Ali was to be raised, we would not have married his wives nor divided his inheritance. But this verse is for people in general."

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abdullah narrated to us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of al-Rabi', regarding His saying ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die﴾: He said: A man from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) swore in the presence of a man from among the deniers, saying: "By He who sends the spirit after death." The other said: "Do you really claim that you will be raised after death?" And he swore by God with his most emphatic oath: "God will not raise up those who die."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, on the authority of Abu Ja'far, on the authority of al-Rabi', on the authority of Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: A man from among the Muslims had a debt owed to him by a man from among the polytheists, so he came to him demanding repayment. Among what he said was: "By He whom I hope for after death, it is such-and-such." The polytheist said: "You claim that you will be raised after death?" And he swore by God with his most emphatic oath: "God will not raise up those who die." So God revealed: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die. Yes indeed! It is a promise binding upon Him, the truth, but most people do not know﴾.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, on the authority of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, that he informed him that he heard Abu Hurayrah say: "God said: The son of Adam reviles Me, and it was not fitting for him to revile Me; and he denies Me, and it was not fitting for him to deny Me. As for his denying Me, he says ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die﴾; I say ﴿Yes indeed!  It is a promise binding upon Him, the truth﴾. As for his reviling Me, he says: ﴿God has taken a son﴾; and I say ﴿Say: He is God, the One. God, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent﴾."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verses 39–41:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars﴾ (39).

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "Rather, Allah will surely resurrect those who die, as a promise binding upon Him, a truth, so that He may make clear to these people, who claim that Allah does not resurrect those who die, and to others who differ concerning it, the revival of His creation after their annihilation; and that those who denied the validity of that and rejected its reality may know that they were liars in their saying: Allah does not resurrect those who die."

As related:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿That He may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾, he said: "For people in general."

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (40) ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place. And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ (41).

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "Indeed, when We intend to resurrect those who die, there is no toil upon Us and no fatigue in reviving them, nor in anything else that We create, produce or bring into being, for when We intend to create and originate it, We only say to it 'Be,' and it is. There is no effort in it and no burden upon Us."

The reciters differed concerning the recitation of His saying "yakun" (it is). Most of the reciters of the Hijaz and Iraq recited it with a nominative ending (fa-yakunu), on the basis of beginning a new sentence, and on the basis that His saying ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, that We say to it, "Be"﴾ is a complete statement, self-sufficient apart from what follows it; then one begins and says: "fa-yakun" (so it is), as the poet said:

*He wishes to make it grammatical, but it makes him foreign* [[This is a line of rajaz verse, one of the witnesses cited by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (p. 161). The point of the line is that the word fa-ya'jimuh is in the nominative, not the subjunctive, is not conjoined to an-yu'riba, but is an independent statement, meaning "so it makes him foreign, and does not make it grammatical." Similar is His saying, "that We say to it 'Be,' so it is" in the nominative, not conjoined to "an naqula." Similar also is His saying, "We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear to them" followed by "fa-yadilla" in the nominative, not the subjunctive as a response to negation. Similar is His saying, "to make clear to you, and We settle in the wombs" with the nominative "naqirru" as a new sentence; and His saying in Bara'ah, "Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands," then He said, "and Allah relents toward whom He wills." Al-Farra' said: When you see a verb in the subjunctive and after it a verb conjoined to it by wa, fa or thumma, if it resembles the meaning of the preceding verb, you conjoin it to it; but if you see that it does not resemble its meaning, you begin anew and make it nominative. From this is his saying: "And poetry, the one who oppresses it cannot master it... he wishes to make it grammatical, but it makes him foreign."]]

Some reciters of the people of Syria and some later reciters of the Kufans recited ﴿fa-yakuna﴾ in the subjunctive, conjoining it to His saying ﴿an naqula lahu﴾. The meaning of the speech according to their view would be: Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is. It has been related from the Arabs by report: "I want to come to you, but rain prevents me," conjoining "yamna'uni" to "ata'ika."

* *

As for His saying ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾:

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "And those who left their people, their homes and their homelands, out of enmity toward them for the sake of Allah, in their disbelief, to others other than them" ﴿after they had been wronged﴾, meaning: after they had been harmed in their persons by hardships for the sake of Allah's essence. ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, meaning: We will surely lodge them in this world in a dwelling that they find pleasing and good.

Concerning this, the people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them﴾, he said: "These are the companions of Muhammad. The people of Makkah wronged them and expelled them from their homes, until groups of them reached Abyssinia. Then Allah settled them in Madinah after that, made it a abode of emigration for them, and made for them helpers from among the believers."

I was told, from al-Qasim ibn Sallam, who said: Hushaym narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi, regarding ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, he said: "Madinah."

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, he said: "They are a people who emigrated to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the people of Makkah after being wronged, and the polytheists wronged them."

Others said: By His saying ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾ is meant: We will surely provide them with good provision in this world.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿We will surely settle them﴾: "We will surely provide them with good provision in this world."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from al-'Awwam, from one who told him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whenever he gave a man among the emigrants his share, would say: "Take it; may Allah bless it for you. This is what Allah promised you in this world, and what He has stored for you in the Hereafter is better." Then he recited this verse: ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾.

The most correct of the two opinions concerning this, in our view, is the view of the one who said: the meaning of ﴿We will surely settle them﴾ is: We will surely cause them to dwell and reside, because al-tabawwu' in the speech of the Arabs is to take up residence in a place and alight in it. From this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a dwelling of truth﴾. It was also said that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl.

Those who said that:

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, who said: "The verse ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged﴾ down to His saying ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl."

* *

As for His saying ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾:

He says: And Allah's reward to them for their emigration therein in the Hereafter is greater, because His reward to them there is the Garden, whose bliss endures and does not perish.

Concerning this, the people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: Allah said ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾, meaning: by Allah, what He rewards them with of His Garden is greater ﴿if they only knew﴾.
