There is no effort in it and no burden upon Us."

The reciters differed concerning the recitation of His saying "yakun" (it is). Most of the reciters of the Hijaz and Iraq recited it with a nominative ending (fa-yakunu), on the basis of beginning a new sentence, and on the basis that His saying ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, that We say to it, "Be"﴾ is a complete statement, self-sufficient apart from what follows it; then one begins and says: "fa-yakun" (so it is), as the poet said:

*He wishes to make it grammatical, but it makes him foreign* [[This is a line of rajaz verse, one of the witnesses cited by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (p. 161). The point of the line is that the word fa-ya'jimuh is in the nominative, not the subjunctive, is not conjoined to an-yu'riba, but is an independent statement, meaning "so it makes him foreign, and does not make it grammatical." Similar is His saying, "that We say to it 'Be,' so it is" in the nominative, not conjoined to "an naqula." Similar also is His saying, "We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear to them" followed by "fa-yadilla" in the nominative, not the subjunctive as a response to negation. Similar is His saying, "to make clear to you, and We settle in the wombs" with the nominative "naqirru" as a new sentence; and His saying in Bara'ah, "Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands," then He said, "and Allah relents toward whom He wills." Al-Farra' said: When you see a verb in the subjunctive and after it a verb conjoined to it by wa, fa or thumma, if it resembles the meaning of the preceding verb, you conjoin it to it; but if you see that it does not resemble its meaning, you begin anew and make it nominative. From this is his saying: "And poetry, the one who oppresses it cannot master it... he wishes to make it grammatical, but it makes him foreign."]]

Some reciters of the people of Syria and some later reciters of the Kufans recited ﴿fa-yakuna﴾ in the subjunctive, conjoining it to His saying ﴿an naqula lahu﴾. The meaning of the speech according to their view would be: Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is. It has been related from the Arabs by report: "I want to come to you, but rain prevents me," conjoining "yamna'uni" to "ata'ika."

* *

As for His saying ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾:

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "And those who left their people, their homes and their homelands, out of enmity toward them for the sake of Allah, in their disbelief, to others other than them" ﴿after they had been wronged﴾, meaning: after they had been harmed in their persons by hardships for the sake of Allah's essence. ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, meaning: We will surely lodge them in this world in a dwelling that they find pleasing and good.

Concerning this, the people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them﴾, he said: "These are the companions of Muhammad. The people of Makkah wronged them and expelled them from their homes, until groups of them reached Abyssinia. Then Allah settled them in Madinah after that, made it a abode of emigration for them, and made for them helpers from among the believers."

I was told, from al-Qasim ibn Sallam, who said: Hushaym narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi, regarding ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, he said: "Madinah."

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, he said: "They are a people who emigrated to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the people of Makkah after being wronged, and the polytheists wronged them."

Others said: By His saying ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾ is meant: We will surely provide them with good provision in this world.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah informed us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿We will surely settle them﴾: "We will surely provide them with good provision in this world."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from al-'Awwam, from one who told him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whenever he gave a man among the emigrants his share, would say: "Take it; may Allah bless it for you. This is what Allah promised you in this world, and what He has stored for you in the Hereafter is better." Then he recited this verse: ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾.

The most correct of the two opinions concerning this, in our view, is the view of the one who said: the meaning of ﴿We will surely settle them﴾ is: We will surely cause them to dwell and reside, because al-tabawwu' in the speech of the Arabs is to take up residence in a place and alight in it. From this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a dwelling of truth﴾. It was also said that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl.

Those who said that:

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, who said: "The verse ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged﴾ down to His saying ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl."

* *

As for His saying ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾:

He says: And Allah's reward to them for their emigration therein in the Hereafter is greater, because His reward to them there is the Garden, whose bliss endures and does not perish.

Concerning this, the people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: Allah said ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾, meaning: by Allah, what He rewards them with of His Garden is greater ﴿if they only knew﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 42:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who were patient and upon their Lord they rely⁠﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: These are the ones whose description We have given, and to whom We have granted the reward We mentioned, those who were patient with God in what befell them in this world. ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾ means: they place their trust in God in their affairs, and they lean on Him in the calamities of affairs that befall them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 43:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾ (16:43).

Allah, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): And We did not send before you, O Muhammad, to any nation among the nations, to call to Our Oneness and to submit to Our command and prohibition, except men from the children of Adam to whom We revealed Our revelation, not angels. That is to say: We sent to your people only the like of what We used to send to those before them among the nations, of their own kind and in their own manner. ﴿So ask the people of the reminder﴾ — that is, He says to the polytheists of Quraysh: And if you do not know that those whom We used to send to those before you among the nations were men from the children of Adam, like Muhammad (ﷺ), and you claimed that they were angels — that is, you supposed that God spoke to them directly — then ask the people of the reminder, who are those who have read the earlier Books: the Torah, the Gospel, and other books of God which He sent down to His servants.

And the interpretation of the commentators is in accordance with what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Waki' narrated to us, he said: al-Muharibi related to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿so ask the people of the reminder﴾, he said: the people of the Torah.

Ibn Waki' narrated to us, he said: al-Muharibi related to us, from Sufyan, who said: I asked al-A'mash about His saying ﴿so ask the people of the reminder﴾, and he said: We have heard that it refers to those among the People of the Torah and the Gospel who embraced Islam. Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj informed me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾, he said: They are the People of the Book.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: 'Ubayd Allah related to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Yahya, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿so ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾, he said: He said to the polytheists of Quraysh: Muhammad is in the Torah and the Gospel.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, he said: Bishr ibn 'Imarah related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Allah sent Muhammad as a messenger, the Arabs denied that, or some of them denied it, and they said: God is greater than to have a messenger who is a human like Muhammad. He said: So Allah sent down ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them?﴾ and He said: ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know, with the clear proofs and the Scriptures﴾. "So ask the people of the reminder": meaning the people of the earlier Books, "Were the messengers who came to you humans or angels? If they were angels, you would deny it; and if they were humans, do not deny that Muhammad is a messenger." He said: Then He said ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns﴾, meaning, they were not from the people of heaven as you claimed.

Others said regarding this:

Ibn Waki' narrated this to us, he said: Ibn Yaman related to us, from Isra'il, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far regarding ﴿so ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾, he said: We are the people of the reminder.

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿so ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾, he said: The reminder is the Qur'an, and he recited ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ (15:9), and he recited ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved in the Reminder when it came to them﴾ (41:41)... the verse.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 44:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures. And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to mankind what has been sent down to them, and that they may reflect﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: We sent men, to whom We revealed, with the clear proofs and the scriptures.

If someone asks: How is it said "with the clear proofs and the scriptures," and what governs this "bi" (the preposition ba') in His words ﴿with the clear proofs﴾? If you say that what governs it is His words ﴿We sent﴾, and it is part of its complement, then is it permissible for the complement of "ma" (the negation particle) before "illa" (except) to come after it? And if you say that what governs it is something other than that, what is it, and where is the verb that governs it? It is said: The grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya) have differed on this. Some of them said: The ba' in His words ﴿bi-l-bayyinat﴾ is part of the complement of "arsalna" (We sent), and "illa" in this position, and with negation and interrogation in every position, means "ghayr" (other than). He said: The meaning of the speech is: "And We did not send before you, with the clear proofs and the scriptures, other than men to whom We revealed." And he would give as an example: "Did not strike except your brother Zayd" and "Did your brother speak to Amr except," meaning: "Did not strike Zayd other than your brother," and "Did your brother speak to Amr except?" He argues for this with the verse of Aws ibn Hajar:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand... except a hand that has no arm."

[[The version of this line in Sibawayh's Kitab (1: 362) is: "O son of Lubayna, you two are not with a hand... except a hand that has no arm," with the hand after "illa" in the accusative, on the basis of the position of the "hand" before it. Al-Shantamari said in commenting on the evidence: The evidence in it is the accusative of what follows "illa," as a substitute (badal) for the position of the ba' and what it governs. The meaning: "You two are not a hand, except a hand that has no arm." The genitive cannot be used as a substitute for the genitive, since what follows "illa" is genitive, and the ba' is an emphasis of the negation. Another version reads: "damaged of arm." Al-Khabl is corruption, i.e., you two are in weakness and lack of benefit like a hand whose arm has been destroyed. End.]]

Al-Farra said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (1: 172): I saw al-Kisa'i make "illa" with negation and interrogation equivalent to "ghayr"... And regarding His words, "If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined" (21:22), he said: I find the meaning only as "If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined." He argued with the words of the poet: "O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand... except a hand that has no arm."

He said: If the meaning were "illa" (the exceptive particle in its ordinary sense), the speech would be corrupt in this sense, because in this verse I cannot restore a governing preposition through a pronoun, and he has gone a different way here.

I say: Shaykh Khalid (al-Azhari) allowed, regarding the "hand" after "illa," the accusative as an exception and as a substitute, as passed in the words of al-A'lam al-Shantamari. He allowed a third view, following al-Kisa'i, and recited the verse as evidence, and this view is that it is in the genitive as an adjective of the first "hand." (Al-Tasrih bi-mudmun al-Tawdih, 1: 424, Amiriyya edition, chapter on exception.)

Shaykh Yasin al-'Ulaymi al-Hims in his gloss on al-Tasrih at this point said: "O sons of Lubayna" in the dual form, as evidenced by his saying "lastuma" (you two are not), i.e., in the narration of the author of al-Tasrih. It is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been omitted, and there is no describing a thing by itself in His saying "illa yad," because the one relied on as an adjective for the first "hand" is the adjective of the second "hand," and the second "hand" is a preparatory (mawti'a) adjective.

He says: If "illa" were not in its own sense, the speech would be corrupt, because the one who put the ba' in the genitive before "illa" cannot restore it after "illa" to put the second "hand" in the genitive. Rather, the meaning of "illa" is the meaning of "ghayr." He also cites the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah...﴾ and says: "illa" here means "ghayr." Another said: This is on two clauses, meaning: "And We did not send before you except men whom We sent with the clear proofs and the scriptures." He said: Likewise the saying of the speaker: "Did not strike except your brother Zayd," meaning: "Did not strike except your brother," then he begins "struck Zayd." Likewise, "Did not pass except your brother by Zayd," meaning "did not pass except your brother," then he says "passed by Zayd." He cites as evidence the verse of al-A'sha:

"He is not one who grants protection if a fearful man comes to the tribe, nor one who speaks except that he is the one who is blamed."

[[The verse is by al-A'sha, Maymun ibn Qays of Banu Tha'laba (his Diwan, Cairo edition, p. 113). He says: He cannot grant safe conduct to a man, placing him under his protection, because people do not respect such protection; they respect only the protection of the strong, so they do not dare to harm their protected one. "Al-mut'ayyab" is a passive participle from "ta'ayyabahu," meaning he attributed defect to him: i.e., nor one who speaks the blameworthy speech except that he is the one. The author has explained how some grammarians (namely al-Kisa'i) used the verse as evidence, and that "al-mut'ayyaba" is in the accusative governed by the omitted "qa'ilan" (speaking). The estimate is: "nor one speaking except he is 'qa'ilan' the blamed." This is the meaning of his statement, but that was permitted on two clauses. End.]]

He says: If that were one utterance it would be wrong, because "al-mut'ayyaba" belongs to the complement of "al-qa'il" (the speaker), but that is permitted on two clauses. Likewise is the saying of another:

"They were informed that they punished their neighbor with fire, and does anyone punish with fire except Allah?"

[[This verse, like the previous one, is evidence that the phrase "bi-l-nar" is part of the complement of the verb "yu'adhdhibu," and what comes before "illa" does not govern what follows it. So it is delayed and one intends two clauses, making "bi-l-nar" a complement of the omitted "yu'adhdhibu." The estimate: "Does anyone punish except Allah, punishing with fire?" The verse is among the evidences cited by al-Farra in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (172).]]

So the interpretation of the speech is then: "And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed; We sent them with the clear proofs and the scriptures, and We sent down to you the Reminder." The "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) are the evidences and arguments which God gave His messengers as proofs of their prophethood, testifying for them to the truth of what they brought to their people from God. The "scriptures" (al-zubur) are the books; it is the plural of "zabur," from "zabartu al-kitab" and "dhabartuhu," meaning: when I wrote the book.

And in the manner of what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have spoken.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾: he said: "al-zubur" means the books.

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to us, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾: he said: the signs (al-ayat). And al-zubur: the books.

- Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: al-Zubur: the books.

- I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿bi-l-zubur﴾: meaning, with the books.

* *

And His words ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder﴾

He says: And We sent down to you, O Muhammad, this Qur'an as a reminder and admonition to people, ﴿that you may make clear to mankind﴾: that is, that you may make them know what has been sent down to them of that, ﴿and that they may reflect﴾: that is, that they may ponder over it and take lesson from it, i.e., from what We sent down to you. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq related to us, saying: al-Thawri related to us, saying: Mujahid said regarding ﴿and that they may reflect﴾: he said: that they may obey.

Commentary on the words of the Exalted: "Do those who plot evil deeds feel secure that Allah will cause the earth to swallow them up, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?" (16:45)

He, exalted is He, says: Do those who wronged the believers among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) feel secure, those who sought to tempt them away from their religion, from the polytheists of Quraysh who said, when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?": "Fables of the ancients" — barring from the path of Allah those who wished to believe in Allah, and turning them away from the right way. [They feel secure] that Allah will cause the earth to swallow them up for their disbelief and polytheism, or that the punishment of Allah will come upon them from a place they do not perceive, not knowing from where it will come to them.

Mujahid said: By this is meant Nimrod ibn Kan'an.

Ḥaddathanī Muḥammad ibn 'Amr, who said: Thanā Abū 'Āṣim, who said: Thanā ʿĪsā. And Ḥaddathanī al-Ḥārith, who said: Thanā al-Ḥasan, who said: Thanā Waqqā'. And Ḥaddathanī al-Muthannā, who said: Thanā Isḥāq, who said: Thanā ʿAbd Allāh, on the authority of Waqqā' — all of them — on the authority of Ibn Abī Najīḥ, on the authority of Mujahid: "Do those who plot evil deeds feel secure that Allah will cause the earth to swallow them up..." ... up to His words "or that He will seize them with gradual wastage" (16:47). He said: It is Nimrod ibn Kan'an and his people.

Ḥaddathanā al-Qāsim, who said: Thanā al-Ḥusayn, who said: Thanī Ḥajjāj, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, the like of it.

We have chosen the interpretation we have stated for this because it is a threat from Allah to the people of polytheism, and it comes right after His words: "We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know" (16:43). Thus a threat directed at those who did not acknowledge the proof of Allah, whose address had run through the preceding discourse, is more fitting than a report about those whose mention has ceased.

Qatada used to say, regarding the meaning of "evil deeds" (al-sayyi'āt) in this place, that it is:

Ḥaddathanā bihi Bishr ibn Mu'ādh, who said: Thanā Yazīd, who said: Thanā Sa'īd, on the authority of Qatada, his statement: "Do those who plot evil deeds feel secure..." — i.e., shirk (polytheism).

The commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro, and they cannot escape [Him]﴾ (16:46) and ﴿Or He seizes them by gradual decline, for indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ (16:47)

His words, exalted is His remembrance, ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾ mean: or He destroys them in their movements through the lands and their wanderings on their journeys. ﴿Then they cannot escape [Him]﴾ means: exalted is His praise, so they cannot escape God from that if He wills to seize them in that way.

What we have said on this is the view of the people of ta'wil (interpretation, i.e. exegesis).

Among those who said this:

Al-Muthanna and Ali ibn Dawud related to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾, he said: If You wish, He seizes them on a journey.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾: in their journeys.

Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada, the same.

Ibn Juraij said regarding this:

Al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾, he said: The taqallub (going to and fro) is that He seizes them by night and by day.

As for His words ﴿Or He seizes them by gradual decline﴾, it means: or He destroys them by gradual reduction, by diminishing from their outskirts and their regions bit by bit until all of them are destroyed. It is said of this: "takhawwafa mal fulan al-infaq" (so-and-so's wealth was diminished by spending) when it is depleted. Similarly, "takhawwafahu" (he took from him gradually) comes from the meaning of tanaqqus (diminution). The poet said:

*He traversed the journey, from her, humped and ... ,*
*As the sanaf (a tool) wears down the wood of a bow-staff.*

The poem is by Ibn Muqbil (Lisan al-Arab, under kh-w-f). He said: al-takhawwuf is tanaqqus (diminution). In the revelation: "Or He seizes them by gradual decline." Al-Farra' said in his tafsir that it means tanaqqus (reduction), and he said: the Arabs say "tahawwaqtuhu," meaning I diminished him from his edges. He said: this is what I have heard, and the tafsir has come with the letter ha'. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also possible that its meaning is: or He seizes them after He frightens them, by destroying a town so that the one next to it becomes afraid. Ibn Muqbil said: takhawwafa... etc. The sanaf is the iron tool with which bows are polished, meaning it diminishes, just as this iron tool eats away the wood of bows. Likewise al-takhwif (causing fear): one says "khawwafahu" and "khawwafa minhu." Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said: "huwa yatahawwafu al-mal" (with the unpointed ha') and "yatakhawwafuhu," meaning he diminishes it and takes from its edges. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "tahawwaftuhu" and "tahayyaftuhu," and "takhawwaftuhu" and "takhayyaftuhu," when one diminishes him. Al-tamik is the hump, or the high hump. Al-qird is one whose hair is gathered, or whose flesh has accumulated from fattening. In Fath al-Qadir by al-Shawkani: al-takhawwuf with the fa' means diminution, a dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. Al-nab' is a tree of the mountains from which bows are made; its singular is nab'a.

By his words "takhawwafa al-sayr" (the journey diminished it) he means: its hump was reduced. We have already mentioned from al-Haytham ibn Adi that he used to say it is a dialect of the Azd Shanu'a, well known among them. And from the words of another:

*Their enemy diminished my wealth and brought [it], chains on the throats, with their clanking.*

This verse is among the evidence cited by Abu Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:360), where he said: "ala takhawwuf" its metaphorical sense is "ala al-tanaqqus" (upon diminution), and he recited two verses, the second being the evidence verse, and the first is:

*I am blamed for satire, and every day there meets me from the neighbours an evil spirit.*

That is, their treachery diminished my wealth. Salasil (chains): he means the rhyming verses that are recited; it is their clanking. It is necklaces on their necks. In the narration of Abu Ubayda and al-Qurtubi it is "ghadrahum" (their treachery) in place of "ʿaduwwahum" (their enemy), that is, their transgression. I say: In Lisan al-Arab also (under kh-w-f): "takhawwanahu" and "khawwanahu" and "khawwana minhu" mean he diminished him. It is said: "takhawwanani fulan haqqi" when so-and-so diminished my right.

Al-Farra' used to say: the Arabs say "tahawwafthu," meaning I diminished him, "tahawwufan," meaning I took him from his edges and extremities. He said: this is what I have heard, and the tafsir has come with the ha', and the two have the same meaning. He said: Similar to it is what has been read in two ways, His words: "Indeed for you in the day is a long span of time (sabhan) and sabkhan (rest)."

What we have said on this is the view of the people of ta'wil.

He said: So he returned to Umar and informed him, and he said: God has decreed that.

* *

And His words ﴿for indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾

He says: indeed your Lord, since He did not seize these who plotted evil deeds with a punishment hastened upon them, and seized some of them by death and diminution one after another, is Most Kind (ra'uf) to His creatures and Most Merciful to them. Out of His kindness and mercy to them He did not cause the earth to swallow them, nor did He hasten punishment upon them, but He frightens them and diminishes them through death.

The commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro, and they cannot escape [Him]﴾ (16:46) and ﴿Or He seizes them by gradual decline, for indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ (16:47)

His words, exalted is His remembrance, ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾ mean: or He destroys them in their movements through the lands and their wanderings on their journeys. ﴿Then they cannot escape [Him]﴾ means: exalted is His praise, so they cannot escape God from that if He wills to seize them in that way.

What we have said on this is the view of the people of ta'wil (interpretation, i.e. exegesis).

Al-Muthanna and Ali ibn Dawud related to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾, he said: If You wish, He seizes them on a journey.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾: in their journeys.

Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada, the same.

Ibn Juraij said regarding this:

Al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding ﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾, he said: The taqallub (going to and fro) is that He seizes them by night and by day.

As for His words ﴿Or He seizes them by gradual decline﴾, it means: or He destroys them by gradual reduction, by diminishing from their outskirts and their regions bit by bit until all of them are destroyed. It is said of this: "takhawwafa mal fulan al-infaq" (so-and-so's wealth was diminished by spending) when it is depleted. Similarly, "takhawwafahu" (he took from him gradually) comes from the meaning of tanaqqus (diminution). The poet said:

*He traversed the journey, from her, humped and ... ,*
*As the sanaf (a tool) wears down the wood of a bow-staff.*

The poem is by Ibn Muqbil (Lisan al-Arab, under kh-w-f). He said: al-takhawwuf is tanaqqus (diminution). In the revelation: "Or He seizes them by gradual decline." Al-Farra' said in his tafsir that it means tanaqqus (reduction), and he said: the Arabs say "tahawwaqtuhu," meaning I diminished him from his edges. He said: this is what I have heard, and the tafsir has come with the letter ha'. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also possible that its meaning is: or He seizes them after He frightens them, by destroying a town so that the one next to it becomes afraid. Ibn Muqbil said: takhawwafa... etc. The sanaf is the iron tool with which bows are polished, meaning it diminishes, just as this iron tool eats away the wood of bows. Likewise al-takhwif (causing fear): one says "khawwafahu" and "khawwafa minhu." Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said: "huwa yatahawwafu al-mal" (with the unpointed ha') and "yatakhawwafuhu," meaning he diminishes it and takes from its edges. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "tahawwaftuhu" and "tahayyaftuhu," and "takhawwaftuhu" and "takhayyaftuhu," when one diminishes him. Al-tamik is the hump, or the high hump. Al-qird is one whose hair is gathered, or whose flesh has accumulated from fattening. In Fath al-Qadir by al-Shawkani: al-takhawwuf with the fa' means diminution, a dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. Al-nab' is a tree of the mountains from which bows are made; its singular is nab'a.

By his words "takhawwafa al-sayr" (the journey diminished it) he means: its hump was reduced. We have already mentioned from al-Haytham ibn Adi that he used to say it is a dialect of the Azd Shanu'a, well known among them. And from the words of another:

*Their enemy diminished my wealth and brought [it], chains on the throats, with their clanking.*

This verse is among the evidence cited by Abu Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:360), where he said: "ala takhawwuf" its metaphorical sense is "ala al-tanaqqus" (upon diminution), and he recited two verses, the second being the evidence verse, and the first is:

*I am blamed for satire, and every day there meets me from the neighbours an evil spirit.*

That is, their treachery diminished my wealth. Salasil (chains): he means the rhyming verses that are recited; it is their clanking. It is necklaces on their necks. In the narration of Abu Ubayda and al-Qurtubi it is "ghadrahum" (their treachery) in place of "ʿaduwwahum" (their enemy), that is, their transgression. The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 48:

The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and to the left, prostrating themselves to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ (16:48)

The reciters differed regarding the recitation of this. The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz, Medina and Basra recited ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا﴾ (awa lam yarawa, "Have they not seen") with the ya' (third person), as a report about those who devised evil deeds (alladhina makaru al-sayyi'at). Some of the reciters of Kufa recited "أوَلم تَرَوا" (awa lam tarawa) with the ta' (second person), as direct address.

The more correct of the two readings in my view is the reading of the one who recites with the ya', as a report about those who devised evil deeds, because this is within the context of their narrative and the report concerning them, and then this report is followed by a report of their turning away from the proof of Allah against them and their neglect of considering His signs and taking lessons from them. The meaning of the speech is therefore: "Have not these who devised evil deeds seen what things Allah has created, any standing object—a tree, a mountain or other than that—whose shadows incline to the right and to the left?" He means: it returns from one place to another; it is at the beginning of the day in one state, then it contracts, then it returns to another state at the end of the day.

Some of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) used to say about "the right and the left" the following:

* Basher narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and to the left, prostrating themselves to Allah﴾: As for "the right," it is the beginning of the day; as for "the left," it is the end of the day.

* Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, with similar wording.

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding ﴿whose shadows incline to the right and to the left﴾: He said: "the morning and the evening (al-ghuduww wa al-asal)," when the shadows incline; the shadows of everything in the morning prostrate to Allah, and when they incline in the evening they prostrate to Allah.

* It was reported to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿whose shadows incline to the right and to the left﴾: meaning, in the mornings and evenings, the shadows prostrate to Allah from morning until the shadow inclines, then they prostrate to Allah until night, meaning: the shadow of every thing.

Ibn 'Abbas used to say regarding His words ﴿whose shadows incline﴾:

* Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih informed us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿whose shadows incline﴾: he said: "they turn/move about" (tatamayyal).

The meaning of His words ﴿prostrating themselves to Allah﴾ was differed upon. Some of them said: the shadow of every thing is its prostration.

Mention of those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿whose shadows incline﴾: He said: the shadow of every thing is its prostration.

* Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Ishaq al-Razi narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Thabit, from al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿whose shadows incline﴾: He said: the shadow of the believer prostrates willingly, and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates unwillingly.

Others said: rather, by His words ﴿whose shadows incline﴾ He means that each of the right and the left, in the state of their prostration; and they said: the prostration of things is other than their shadows.

Mention of those who said that:

* Ibn Humayd and Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Awdi narrated to us, both saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Thabit, from al-Dahhak, regarding the words of Allah ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline﴾: He said: when the shade inclines, every thing turns prostrating towards the qiblah, whether plant or tree. He said: they used to recommend prayer at that time.

* Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hammani informed us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah ﴿whose shadows incline﴾: He said: when the sun declines, every thing prostrates to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Others said: rather, what Allah described with prostration in this verse is the shadows of things, so it is only their shadows that prostrate, not that to which the shadows belong.

Mention of those who said that:

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline﴾: He said: it is the prostration of the shadows, the shadows of every thing that is in the heavens and on the earth, of every creature. He said: the prostration of the shadows of animals and the shadows of every thing.

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline﴾: "what Allah has created of every thing, to its right and its left"; so the word "ma" is singular in wording, and he said: Did you not see that when you pray the dawn prayer, what is between the rising of the sun and its setting is a shadow; then Allah sends the sun as a guide over it, and Allah withdraws the shadow.

The most correct of these statements, in my view, is to say: Allah informs in this verse that the shadows of things are what prostrate, and their prostration is their inclining and turning from side to side, and from direction to direction, as Ibn 'Abbas said. It is said of this: "the date palm prostrated" when it leaned, and "the camel prostrated and was made to prostrate" when it was made to bow down for riding. We have already explained the meaning of prostration in another place, in a manner sufficient to avoid repeating it here.

* *

As for His words ﴿and they are humbled﴾:

He means: "and they are abased (sagirun)." It is said from it: "Fulan dakhara li-Allah, yadkharu dakhran wa dukhuran" when he was humbled and submitted to Him. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"There remained only one humbled in the enclosure, and one hiding in a burrow other than your land, in a hole."

[[The line is evidence that the meaning of "dakhir" is "sagir" (abased). Abu 'Ubayda said in Majaz al-Qur'an: "wa hum dakhirun": i.e., abased; it is said: "Fulan dakhar li-Allah": i.e., he was humbled and submitted. In (al-Lisan: dakhar): "dakhara al-rajulu" (with fatha) yadkharu dakhuran, so he is dakhir, and dakhara dakharan (like fariha) was humbled and became small, yasghar sighaaran, and he is the one who does what he is commanded, willingly or unwillingly, abased and contemptible. In (al-Lisan: khays): every prison is "mukhays" and "mukhayyas" (with the yaa' doubled, fatha and kasra). He recited the line and attributed it to al-Farazdaq. Al-munjahir: the one who enters a burrow; it is said: "ajhara" and "fa-injahara": he made it enter the burrow, so it entered. Al-juhr: everything that vermin and beasts despise for themselves. Its plural: ajhar and juhra.]]

And according to what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation said.

Mention of those who said that:

* Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, "and they are humbled": sagirun (abased).

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* Basher narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, "and they are humbled": i.e., sagirun (abased).

* Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, the like of it.

As for the singular of "the right" in His words ﴿from the right and the left﴾ while it is collected (in the plural form for the left), this is because the meaning of the speech is: "Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline from its right"—i.e., the right of what Allah has created—"and its left." So the word "ma" is singular in form, but its meaning is plural. He said "from the right" meaning "from the right of what is created," then he returned to its meaning for the left. Some of the people of Arabic grammar said: the Arabs do this because most speech is addressed to one individual, so it is said to a man: "Take from your right." He said: when it is singular, it refers to one of the people; and when it is plural, it is that in which there is no questioning. He cited as evidence for the Arabs' practice the words of the poet:

"Let the stone be in the mouths of the scoffers, if the calamity of the two cubs of a lioness in the lions has broken me."

[[This line is among the evidences of al-Farra' in (Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 172), cited when discussing the verse "yatafayya'u zilaluhu 'an al-yamini wal-shama'il". He said: the shadow returns on everything from its sides, and that is its tafayyu'; then he explained, saying: "from the right and the left," and all of that is permissible in Arabic. The poet said: "bi-fi al-shamitin..." (the line). He said he did not say "bi-afwah al-shamitin" (in the mouths of the scoffers, plural of mouth). I say: he means that the plural "al-shama'il" with singular "al-yamin" is permissible in Arabic, and he cited the line as evidence. The author has given a fine explanation in the tafsir.]]

So he said: "bi-fi al-shamitin" (in the mouth of the scoffers), and did not say "bi-afwah" (in the mouths); and the other's saying:

"The arrivers, and Taym in the heights of Saba, the hide of buffaloes has bitten their necks."

[[This line too, like the one before it, is among al-Farra's evidences (in Ma'ani al-Qur'an, after the previous one, 1: 172), that the poet said "jild al-jawamis" with the singular, and did not say "julud al-jawamis," in correspondence with "a'naqahum" (their necks). We have not found the line in the references, nor its speaker.]]

He did not say: "julud" (hides, plural).

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant﴾ (49).

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And to Allah humbles itself and submits to His command whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures that move upon it, and the angels who are in the heavens, and they are not arrogant to abase themselves before Him in obedience. ﴿But those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant﴾ [cf. 16:22]. And their shadows incline from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled [cf. 16:48].

Some of the grammarians of Basra used to say: "He has made do with mentioning one of the creatures (dawabb) in place of mentioning all of them." The meaning of the statement is: "And to Allah prostrate whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures and the angels," just as one says: "There came to me from a man (ma atani min rajul)," meaning: "There came to me from men."

Some of the grammarians of Kufa used to say: "It was only said *min dabbah* (of a creature) because *ma* (what), although it may take the sense of *alladhi* (that which), is not specific. When it is used in an unspecified way, it resembles the conditional, and the conditional admits *min* before the indefinite noun that follows it, so one says: *man darabahu min rajul fa-idribuhu* ('whoever strikes him, of a man, then strike him'). *Min* is not dropped from this position, lest it be likened to a circumstantial state (hal) for *man* and *ma*. Rather, they placed *min* so as to indicate that it is an explanation of *ma* and *man*, since both are unspecified. Thus the entry of *min* after them was an explanation of their meaning, and the entry of *min* was more indicative of what is unspecified than *min* and *ma*; for that reason, neither of them was made void."

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and do what they are commanded﴾ (16:50)**

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: These angels who are in the heavens, and whatever creature crawls upon the earth, fear their Lord above them, lest He punish them if they disobey His command. ﴿And do what they are commanded﴾ means: they do what God has commanded them, so they discharge His rights and avoid His wrath.

* *

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, ﴿And God said: Do not take two gods. He is only one God. So fear Me alone﴾ (16:51)**

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: God said to His servants: Do not take a partner for Me, O people, and do not worship two objects of worship. For if you worship another alongside Me, you have made a partner for Me, and I have no partner. He is only one God and one object of worship, and I am that. ﴿So fear Me alone﴾ means: so fear and dread My punishment by disobeying Me, if you disobey Me and worship other than Me, or associate a partner with Me in your worship.

* *

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him is religion, ever-lasting. Will you then fear other than God?﴾ (16:52)**

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: To God belongs the dominion of whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and He has no partner in any of it. He is the One who created them, He is the One who provides for them, and in His hand is their life and their death.

* *

As for His words, ﴿And to Him is religion, wasiban﴾:

God, may His praise be exalted, says: To Him belongs obedience and sincerity, constant, established and obligatory. It is said of this root: wasiba al-dinu yasibu wusuban and wasban, as al-Dili (al-Du'ali) said:

*I do not seek a little praise whose endurance*

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 53:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah. Then, when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help.﴾

The grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyya, the scholars of Arabic grammar) differed over the reason the fa' (the particle "then/so", fa') enters His words ﴿fa-mina Allah﴾. Some of the Basran grammarians said: the fa' entered because "ma" (whatever) has the status of "man" (whoever), so the predicate is introduced with the fa'. Some of the Kufan grammarians said: "ma" carries the meaning of a conditional (jaza', the conditional sense), and it has an implied verb, as if you had said: "Whatever blessing may be among you, it is from Allah," because the conditional must have a jussive verb; if it appears, it is jussive, and if it does not appear, it is implied, as the poet said:

"If intellect (al-'aql) in our wealth, we do not constrict with it a forearm's length, and if patience, we recognize for patience..."

[[The verse is one of the witnesses cited by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (1: 173) at His words, "Whatever blessing you have is from Allah." He said: "ma" has the sense of a conditional, and it has an implied verb, as if you had said: "Whatever blessing may be among you, it is from Allah," because the conditional must have a jussive verb; if it appears, it is jussive, and if it does not appear, it is implied, as the poet said: "If intellect..." the verse. He meant: "If there be," and he omitted it. If you make "ma bikum" in the sense of "alladhi" (which), it is permissible, and its relative clause is "bikum," and "alladhi" is then in the nominative position, governed by "fa-mina Allah." He introduced the fa', as He, may He be exalted, said: "Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you (inna al-mawta alladhi tafirruna minhu fa-innahu mulaqikum)." Every relative noun, such as man, ma, and alladhi, may take the fa' in its predicate, because it resembles the conditional. "Al-'aql" in the verse means: the blood-money (diya).]]

He also said: He meant, "If the intellect is there," and He omitted it. He said: If you make "ma bikum" in the sense of "alladhi," it is permissible, and you make its relative clause "bikum," with "ma" in the nominative position governed by "fa-mina Allah," and you introduce the fa', as He said: ﴿Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you﴾. Every relative noun, such as man, ma, and alladhi, may take the fa' in its predicate, because it resembles the conditional, and the conditional may be answered with the fa'. But you may not say "akhuka fa-huwa qa'im" ("your brother, so he is standing"), because it is not a relative noun. Similarly you say "malaka li" (what is yours is for me); if you say "malaka," you may say "malaka fa-huwa li," and if you drop the fa', it is correct.

The meaning of the statement is: Whatever may be among you, O people, in your bodies of wellbeing, health and soundness, and in your wealth of increase, it is Allah who has bestowed it upon you, not other than Him, because that belongs to Him and is in His hand. ﴿Then, when adversity touches you﴾ means: when sickness and illness affect your bodies, a passing ailment, or hardship of life, ﴿to Him you cry for help﴾ means: to Allah you cry out in supplication and seek His aid, so that He removes that from you. Its origin is from the bellowing of a bull (ju'ar al-thawr); it is said of it: "the bull bellowed (ja'ara al-thawru yaj'aru ju'aran)," when it raises a loud voice from hunger or other cause. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And not the monk (al-Ayyili) upon the shrine (haykal) that he built, and crucified (salaba) in it and carved (sara)... alternating between the prayers of the king, at times prostrating and at times crying out (ju'aran)."

[[The two verses are from the poetry of al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays (his Diwan, Cairo edition, p. 53), from an ode of seventy verses in praise of Qays ibn Ma'dikarib. Al-Ayyili: the monk who owns the ayyil, the staff with which the bell is struck. Al-Haykal: a place in the front of the church, close to the offering. Salaba: he carved the cross in it. In Lisan al-'Arab: sara. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi related "sara" (carved). It seems to me that what is meant by "sara" in the verse is what al-A'sha said in another verse, in describing wine: "and prayed over its jar and made the sign (irtasama)." Irtasama means: he pointed with his hand to his forehead, heart and chest, right and left, as the Christians do. Rawaha between the two acts: alternated this at one time and that at another. Ja'ara ila Allah ju'aran: he humbly called upon Him with supplication and pleading. He says: the monk secluded in his shrine before his cross, constant in his prayers, prostrating and humbly calling upon Allah, is not greater than him in piety in reckoning (the predicate of "ma" is in the verse after the two verses).]] By al-ju'ar is meant: crying out, either by supplication or by recitation.

Ahl al-ta'wil (the scholars of interpretation) said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa informed us, saying: Shibl told us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: 'Abd Allah told us, from Warqa', all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿to Him you cry for help﴾: he said: you humbly supplicate.

- al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih informed us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: al-Darr (adversity): al-suqm (sickness).

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verses 54–55:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord,﴾ ﴿so that they may deny what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾

His, may He be remembered, saying: Then when your Lord grants you well-being, removes from you the illness that afflicted your bodies and the hardship in your livelihood, and relieves you of the trial, ﴿behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord﴾ means: behold, a group of you make partners with God in their worship, so they worship idols and slaughter sacrifices to them, giving thanks to other than the One who bestowed upon them relief from the harm they were in. ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them﴾ means: so that they may deny God's blessing in what He gave them by removing the harm from them. ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾: this is a threat and warning from God to those whose attributes He described in these verses. He, may His majesty be praised, says to them: Enjoy this worldly life until your appointed times reach you and you attain the term He has set for your life and your enjoyment of it, for you will then surely return to your Lord, and you will come to know the consequence of what your hands have earned, and you will recognize the evil outcome of your affair, and you will regret when regret will not benefit you.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 56:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they assign to that which they know not a portion of what We have provided for them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾

His saying, exalted is He, means: These polytheists, the worshippers of idols, assign to that which neither harms nor benefits them a portion. He says: a share and a due from the wealth We have provided them, associating it with Him, while they know that it is He who created them, and it is He who benefits and harms them, not other than Him.

As related:

* Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿And they assign to that which they know not a portion of what We have provided for them﴾: He said: They know that Allah created them and that He harms and benefits them, and then they assign to what they do not know to harm or benefit them a portion of what We have provided for them.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And they assign to that which they know not a portion of what We have provided for them﴾: They are the polytheists of the Arabs. They assigned to their idols a portion of what We provided them, and a part of their wealth which they set aside for their idols.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿And they assign to that which they know not a portion of what We have provided for them﴾: They assigned to their gods, which have no portion or anything, a portion of what Allah mentioned of the tilth and the livestock, naming their names over it and slaughtering for them.

* * *

And His saying ﴿By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate﴾

His saying, exalted is He, means: By Allah, O polytheists who set up gods and rivals and assign a portion of what We have provided you to them, in association with Allah and disbelief, Allah will surely question you on the Day of Resurrection about what you used to fabricate in the world, meaning: what you invented of falsehood and lies against Allah by claiming a partner for Him, and by designating a portion of what He provided you for your idols. Then He will surely punish you with a punishment that is a recompense for your ingratitude toward His blessings and your fabrication against Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 57–58:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They attribute to Allah daughters—glory be to Him!—and for themselves what they desire.﴾ (57) ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ (58)

The Exalted says: And consider the ignorance of these polytheists, the evil of their deed, and the ugliness of their fabrication against their Lord: that they attribute to the One who created them, provided for them, and bestowed blessings upon them—who thereby deserves their gratitude and is worthy of their praise—daughters. It is not fitting for Allah to have any offspring, male or female; glory be to Him. The Majestic, the Mighty, has declared Himself free of what they ascribed to Him and attributed to Him of daughters. Yet they were not content, in their ignorance, to ascribe to Him what is not fitting for Him to be ascribed, nor what is fitting for Him to have of offspring; they ascribed to Him what they themselves dislike and would not accept for themselves, namely daughters, whom they would kill if they were theirs.

Regarding the "mā" in His saying ﴿and for themselves what they desire﴾, there are two possibilities from the standpoint of Arabic grammar. The first is the accusative (naṣb), coordinating it with "daughters"; in that case the meaning of the statement, if this is intended, is: "They attribute to Allah daughters, and for themselves the sons they desire," so that "mā" refers to the sons. The second is the nominative (raf'), treating the statement as a new sentence beginning with His saying ﴿and for themselves what they desire﴾; the meaning then is: "They attribute to Allah daughters, and for themselves are sons."

* *

As for His saying ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of a female, his face becomes dark﴾:

It means: when one of those who attribute daughters to Allah is given the good news of the birth of what they ascribe to Him of that kind, his face becomes dark from his aversion to it. ﴿And he is filled with suppressed grief﴾: he says, he has held back (kaẓama) the sorrow and is filled with distress at his birth of her, so he does not show it.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said what is similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas (regarding) ﴿They attribute to Allah daughters—glory be to Him!—and for themselves what they desire﴾, then He said ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ ... to the end of the verse. He says: "They attribute to Allah daughters, which you accept for Me, and you do not accept for yourselves." That is because in the pre-Islamic period, when a man among them had a girl born to him, he would keep her in humiliation, or bury her alive in the dust.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾: This is the practice of the polytheist Arabs. Allah, the Exalted, informed them of the evil of their practice. As for the believer, he ought to be content with what Allah has apportioned for him, and Allah's decree is better than a person's decree for himself. By my life, he does not know that it is better: many a girl is better for her family than a boy. Allah has only informed you of their practice so that you avoid it and refrain from it. One of them would feed his dog and bury his daughter.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said regarding ﴿and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾: "Sorrowful."

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Awn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying ﴿and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾: "al-kazim: the one who is grieved (al-kamid)." We have explained this with its evidences in another place.
