The Exegesis of His words, the Exalted: ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil of that whereof he has been given tidings. Shall he keep it in humiliation or bury it in the dust? Certainly evil is what they judge.﴾ (16:59)

He, the Exalted, says: This one who is given tidings of the birth of a female child hides himself from the people, so that he is hidden from their sight, ﴿because of the evil of that whereof he has been given tidings﴾, meaning: because of the distress it causes him, wavering between keeping her in humiliation (ʿalā hūn), that is, in disgrace (hawān). This is also the usage of the Quraysh, as has been related to me: they say hawn for humiliation. From this is the verse of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:

"When I feared humiliation (al-hawn), while the donkey was held,
Upon its disgrace, the rope was set firm by its hoof."

[The verse is in the Diwan of al-Ḥuṭayʾa, printed in Cairo by al-Taqaddum, p. 10. Its commentator said: he means that as long as the donkey is tethered, it is humbled, acknowledging its humiliation. This is an inversion; he intended: "what the hoof fixed the rope," (the rope is the subject of "fixed," and the hoof is the object), so it was inverted, making the subject an object and the object a subject. Similar to it is: "They surrendered her in Damascus as Wahshiyya surrendered the noose," meaning: as Wahshiyya surrendered the noose (al-wahq: a rope with a slipknot, by which an animal or a person is caught; its plural is awhāq). And ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward said: "Had I witnessed Abu Saʿd, on the morning he set out with his life at stake... I would have ransomed his soul with my soul and my wealth, and I would not fall short of doing all that I can." That is, I would not leave off any effort. He intended: "I would have ransomed his soul with my soul," and so inverted it.]

Some of the Banu Tamim used hawn as the verbal noun for the thing that is easy (hayyin). Al-Kisaʾi mentioned that he heard them say: "You are indeed of little burden (hawn al-muʾna) since today." He said: I also heard hawan used in this same sense; I heard a speaker say of a camel of his: "There is nothing wrong with it except its hawan," meaning, it is of light value. When they say "he walks upon his hawn," they only say it with the letter hāʾ vocalized with a fatḥa, as God says: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾.

﴿Or bury it in the dust﴾: he says, he buries her alive in the dust, burying her alive.

As has been said:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding ﴿Shall he keep it in humiliation or bury it in the dust?﴾: he buries his daughter alive.

And His words, ﴿Certainly evil is what they judge﴾

He says: Evil is the judgment that these polytheists make, for they ascribed to God what they do not like for themselves, and they assigned to what neither benefits nor harms them a share in what God has provided them, and they worshipped other than the One who created them and bestowed favour upon them.

The Interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness; and to Allah belongs the highest likeness. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise⦆ (16:60)

This is a report from Allah, may His praise be exalted, that His words ﴿When one of them is given good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief⦆ [16:58], and the verse that follows it, are a likeness which Allah has struck for these polytheists who attributed daughters to Allah. By His words ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness⦆ He clarified that it is a likeness. By His words, may His praise be exalted, ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter⦆ He means: for those among the polytheists who do not affirm the return, the reward and the punishment. ﴿The evil likeness⦆ means the ugly kind of likeness, and whatever is evil for the one to whom that likeness is struck. ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest likeness⦆ means: and to Allah belongs the highest likeness, which is the most excellent, the finest, the best and the most beautiful, and that is the affirmation of His oneness and submission to Him, that there is no god other than Him.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿and to Allah belongs the highest likeness⦆, he said: It is the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

• Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness⦆: sincerity (ikhlas) and monotheism (tawhid).

* *

As for His words ﴿And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise⦆

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Allah is the Possessor of might, by which none can prevent Him from punishing these polytheists whose attributes He has described in these verses, nor from punishing whomever He wills for disobeying Him. Nothing He wills or decrees is beyond His power, because creation is His creation and command is His command. He is Wise in His management, so no flaw or error enters His management.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 61:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature moving upon it﴾ [16:61] ...

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task﴾ — the disobedient among the children of Adam — ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ — for their sins — ﴿He would not leave upon it﴾ — meaning upon the earth — ﴿a single creature moving upon it﴾ — crawling on it. ﴿But He defers them﴾ — that is, He says: but by His forbearance He defers these wrongdoers and does not hasten to punish them — ﴿until an appointed term﴾ — that is, until their time, which has been set for them. ﴿So when their term comes﴾ — that is, when the time set for their destruction arrives — ﴿they cannot delay it by an hour﴾ — from destruction — so that they are given respite — ﴿nor can they advance it﴾ — until they have fulfilled their terms.

Scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said things in accordance with what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, who said: The dung beetle (al-ju'l) almost gets punished for the sin of the children of Adam. And he recited: ﴿If Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾.

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Hakim al-Khuza'i narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jabir al-Ju'fi narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Abu Salamah, who said: Abu Hurayrah heard a man saying: Indeed the wrongdoer harms only himself. He said: So he turned to him and said: Yes indeed, by Allah, the houbara bustard dies in its nest from the starvation caused by the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer.

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Ubaydah al-Haddad narrated to us, saying: Qurrah ibn Khalid al-Sadusi narrated to us, from al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi, who said: Ibn Mas'ud said: The sin of the son of Adam killed the dung beetle.

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu 'Ubaydah, who said: 'Abd Allah said: The dung beetle almost perished in its burrow because of the sin of the son of Adam.

Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, regarding Allah's saying: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾, who said: We hold that when their term has arrived, it is not delayed an hour nor advanced, but as long as their term has not arrived, Allah defers whomever He wills and advances whomever He wills.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues utter the lie that for them is the best. Undoubtedly for them is the Fire, and they will be left behind [or: neglected].﴾ (16:62)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: And these polytheists attribute to Allah what they themselves dislike. ﴿And their tongues utter the lie﴾ means: their tongues say the lie and fabricate it, that for them is the best (al-husna). Here "that" (anna) is in the accusative position, because it is an explanation (tarjama) of "the lie." The meaning of the statement is: they attribute to Allah what they dislike for themselves, and they claim that for them is the best, which they dislike for themselves. They attribute daughters to Allah, the Exalted, and they claimed that the angels are daughters of Allah. As for "the best" which they reserved for themselves: it is male offspring, because they used to bury their female children alive and keep the males, saying: "For us are the males, and for Allah the daughters." This is similar to His saying: ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters, glory be to Him, and for themselves what they desire﴾.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us. And al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa informed us, saying: Shibl related to us. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abd Allah related to us, from Warqa, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And their tongues utter the lie that for them is the best﴾: he said: It is the saying of Quraysh: "For us are the sons, and for Allah the daughters."

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same, except that he said: It is the saying of the disbelievers of Quraysh.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues utter the lie﴾: that is, they speak that for them is the best, i.e., the boys.

- Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿that for them is the best﴾: he said: The boys.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Undoubtedly for them is the Fire, and they will be left behind [or: neglected]﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Truly, it is a binding certainty that for these speakers who attribute daughters to Allah, who assign to Him what they dislike for themselves, and for themselves is the best with Allah on the Day of Resurrection, is the Fire.

We have already explained the interpretation of Allah's saying ﴿Undoubtedly (la jaram)﴾ in other places in this book with its evidences, so there is no need to repeat it here.

It was narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding it:

- al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿la jaram﴾: he said: It means "yes" (bala).

* *

And His saying: ﴿la jaram﴾

Some of the grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyya) said: jaram is not put in the accusative by "la" as the "m" is put in the accusative in the saying "la ghulam laka" (there is no boy for you). Rather, it is in the accusative because it is a past-tense verb, like the saying of a speaker: "qa'ada fulan" and "jalasa" (so-and-so sat). The meaning of the sentence: "la radda li-kalamihim" (there is no rejection of their speech), i.e., the matter is not thus. Jaram means "kasaba" (earned), like His saying "la uqsimu" (I do not swear), and similar. Some of them said: jaram is in the accusative by "la," and it means "la budda" (there is no escape) and "la mahala" (without doubt); but it became frequent in speech until it took the place of "haqqan" (truly).

* *

And His saying: ﴿And they will be left behind [or: neglected]﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: And they are left behind, abandoned in the Fire, forgotten therein.

The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of this. Most of them said something similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar and Ibn Wakic related to us, both saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, saying: Shu'ba related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding this verse ﴿Undoubtedly for them is the Fire, and they will be left behind﴾: he said: forgotten, neglected.

- Musa ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Masruqi related to me, saying: Zayd ibn Habbab related to us, saying: Sa'id informed us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the same.

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Bahz ibn Asad related to us, from Shu'ba, saying: Abu Bishr informed me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the same.

- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Abu Bishr informed us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿Undoubtedly for them is the Fire, and they will be left behind﴾: he said: left behind in the Fire, forgotten therein.

- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Husayn informed us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, with the like.

- al-Muthanna related to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal informed us, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, with the like.

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding ﴿And they will be left behind﴾: he said: forgotten.

- al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us; and al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa informed us, saying: Shibl related to us; and al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abd Allah related to us, from Warqa, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

- Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: Abda, Abu Mu'awiya and Abu Khalid related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿And they will be left behind﴾: he said: left behind in the Fire.

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from al-Qasim, from Mujahid regarding ﴿left behind﴾: he said: forgotten.

- Abd al-Warith ibn Abd al-Samad related to me, saying: my father related to me, from al-Husayn, from Qatada regarding ﴿And they will be left behind﴾: he says: neglected.

- Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Badal related to us, saying: Abbad ibn Rashid related to us, saying: I heard Dawud ibn Abi Hind, regarding Allah's saying ﴿And they will be left behind﴾: he said: forgotten in the Fire.

Others said: the meaning of that is: they are hastened to the Fire, sent forward to it, and they went in that direction to the saying of the Arabs: "afratna fulanan fi talab al-ma'" (we sent so-and-so ahead in seeking water) when they send him ahead to repair the buckets and ropes and prepare what they need upon their arrival at it; he is then "mufrat." As for the one who precedes others himself, he is "farit." It is said: "qad farata fulan ashabahu yafruthuhum furtan wa furutan" (so-and-so went ahead of his companions) when he precedes them; and the plural of farit is "furrat." From this is al-Qutami's saying:

*wastaʿjalūnā wa-kānū min ṣaḥābatinā*
*kamā taʿajjala furrāṭun li-wurrādi*

[The verse is in the Diwan of al-Qutami (Leiden ed. 1902), where it reads "fa-ista'jalunā" with fa. He says: "ista'jalūnā" meaning "a'jalūnā" (hastened us), he means they preceded us; al-furrat are those who precede the arriving group, repairing the ropes, until the people come after them. In Lisan al-Arab: "farata": "farata al-qawm yafruthuhum furtan" and "faratah" means preceding them to the watering place to repair ropes and buckets, and clearing the basins and watering in them; so I am "farit" and they are "furrat." In al-Sihah: "kama ta'ajjala" means "kama taqaddama" (as he went ahead).]

And from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I am your farat at the Pool," meaning: I am your precursor to it and your forerunner, "until you come to it."

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada regarding ﴿And they will be left behind﴾: he says: hastened to the Fire.

- Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada regarding ﴿And they will be left behind﴾: he said: they have been sent ahead into the Fire, i.e., hastened.

Others said: the meaning of that is: they are removed far away in the Fire.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: my father related to us, from Ashath al-Sammān, from al-Rabi', from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id regarding ﴿And they will be left behind﴾: he said: cast down and removed far away.

The most correct of these opinions in terms of truth is the view we have chosen. This is because "ifrat" in the sense of "sending ahead" is only said of one who is sent ahead to prepare what is sent to him until the time when the one who sent him arrives; and the one sent into the Fire from its people is not sent ahead to repair anything in it for an arriving person who will come to it and be served there by him. Rather, whoever is sent into it is sent for a punishment that is hastened upon him. Since the meaning of that "ifrat," which is the interpretation of hastening, is untenable as correct, the other meaning is established: "ifrat" in the sense of leaving behind and abandoning. It is related from the Arabs: "ma afratu wara'i ahadan" (I did not leave anyone behind me), i.e., I did not leave him; and "ma farratuhu" (I did not leave him behind).

The readers differed regarding the recitation of this. The readers of the two cities, Kufa and Basra, generally recited ﴿wa-annahum mufratūn﴾ with the "r" lightened and vowelled with a fatha, according to the meaning of the passive form: "uflita (fa-huwa mufrat)" (one who is neglected). I have explained the difference in recitation of it in this way in the interpretation. Abu Ja'far the reader recited "wa-annahum mufarritūn" with the "r" kasra and doubled, with the interpretation: they are neglectful in fulfilling the obligation Allah had upon them in the world, of obedience and His rights, losing those, from Allah's saying ﴿O my regret over what I neglected concerning the side of Allah﴾. And Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym recited "wa-annahum mufrituna" with the "r" kasra and lightened.

- Younus related to me, from Warsh, from him, with the interpretation: they are excessive in sins and transgressions, extravagant against themselves and multiplying them, from the saying "afrata fulan fi al-qawl" when someone exceeds his limit and goes to excess in it.

The most correct of the recitations in this matter is the recitation of those whose recitation we mentioned from the people of Iraq, because it agrees with the interpretation of the people of interpretation which we mentioned before, and the other recitations depart from their interpretation.

By Allah, We certainly sent messengers to communities before you (O Muhammad), and Satan made their deeds appear fair to them, so he is their ally today, and theirs is a painful punishment. (63)

Allah, exalted is His remembrance, says, swearing by Himself, the Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): By Allah, O Muhammad, We certainly sent messengers before you to their communities, with the same message with which We sent you to your community: calling to the Oneness of Allah, sincerely devoting worship to Him, submitting to Him in obedience, and renouncing rivals and false gods. ﴿So Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾ means: Satan made attractive to them what they were upon of disbelief in Allah and worship of idols, persisting in it, until they denied their messengers and rejected what their messengers brought to them from their Lord. ﴿So he is their ally today﴾ means: Satan is their helper today in this world, and what an evil helper he is. ﴿And theirs is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter, upon their arrival before their Lord. On that day the alliance of Satan will benefit them not, nor did it benefit them in this world; rather it harmed them in it, and in the Hereafter it will be more harmful to them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 64:

The explanation of His saying, ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ, and as a guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet ﷺ: And We have not sent down to you, O Muhammad, Our Book, nor have We sent you as a messenger to Our creation, except that you may make clear to them what they differ about of the religion of God, so that you may inform them of the correct part of it and of truth from falsehood, and establish upon them, through the correct part of it, the proof of God with which He sent you.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾:

He says: and as guidance, meaning clarification from misguidance, referring by that to the Book, and as mercy for a people who believe in it, who affirm what is in it, acknowledge what it contains of God's command and prohibition, and act upon it. The phrase "guidance" is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the position of "li-yubayyina" (so that he may make clear), because its position is accusative (naṣb). The meaning of the sentence is: And We have not sent down the Book to you except as a clarification for the people of what they differ about, and as guidance and mercy.

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah sends down water from the sky, and by it revives the earth after its death. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says, alerting His creation to His proofs against them concerning His oneness, and that divinity is not befitting except to Him, and worship is not suitable for anything other than Him: O people, your deity, to whom worship is due above all things, ﴿sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: rain. He says: by means of the water sent down from the sky He causes to grow on the dead earth, which has no crops, no herbage and no vegetation, ﴿after its death﴾, after it had become dead with nothing in it. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾. He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: indeed, in Our reviving the earth after its death by the water We send down from the sky, there is a clear proof and a decisive argument, an excuse for whoever reflects upon it. ﴿for a people who listen﴾ means: for a people who hear this statement, ponder it and understand it, and obey Allah by what it guides them to.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed in the livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, from between digestive contents and blood, pure milk, palatable to those who drink.﴾ (16:66)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And indeed, O people, there is a admonition for you in the livestock, which We give you to drink from what is in their bellies.

The reciters differed over the reading of His words ﴿nusqīkum﴾. The people of Makkah, Iraq, Kufa and Basra, except ʿĀṣim, recited it, and from the people of Madinah Abū Jaʿfar recited ﴿nusqīkum﴾ with a damma on the nūn. The meaning is that He made them drink a continuous drink. al-Kisāʾī used to say: the Arabs say "asqaynāhum nahran" and "asqaynāhum laban" when they make it a constant drink, but when they mean that they gave them a single drink, they say "saqaynāhum," with no alif. The majority of the reciters of Madinah, except Abū Jaʿfar, and from the people of Iraq ʿĀṣim, recited ﴿naslqīkum﴾ with a fatḥa on the nūn, from saqāhu Allāh, so that he (saqā) yasqīhi. The Arabs may bring in the alif for what is not constant drinking and omit it for what is constant, although the more well-known usage among them is what al-Kisāʾī said. What supports what we have said is the verse of Labīd describing a cloud:

*Saqā qawmī Banī Majdin wa-asqā ... Numayran wal-qabā'ila min Hilāl*

[The verse is by Labīd (Lisān al-ʿArab: saqā). He said: al-saqy is well known, and the noun is al-suqyā with a ḍamma. God gave them rain (saqāhu al-ghayth) and made them drink it (asqāhu). Labīd combined both in his words "saqā qawmī." al-Farrāʾ said in Maʿānī al-Qurʾān (174): the Arabs say of whatever comes from the bellies of livestock and from the sky, or a river flowing for a people: asqaytu. When a man gives you water to wet your lips, they say saqāhu and do not say asqāhu, as God the Mighty and Majestic said: "and their Lord gave them a pure drink" and He said: "who feeds me and gives me drink." They sometimes say of what is in the bellies of livestock and of rainwater: saqā al-samāʾ and asqā, as Labīd said: "saqā qawmī..." the verse. The reciters differed; some recited nusqīkum and some yusqīkum.]

So both dialects are combined in one meaning. If that is so, then whichever of the two readings the reciter uses is correct. However, the reading with a ḍamma on the nūn is more preferable to me, for the reason I mentioned: the more common usage among the Arabs for a continuous giving of drink is asqā with an alif, so it is yusqī, and what God gives His servants to drink from the bellies of livestock is a continuous provision for them that does not cease.

As for His words ﴿mimmā fī buṭūnihi﴾ (from what is in their bellies), although livestock (al-anʿām) was mentioned earlier, and it is plural, while the pronoun in "buṭūn" is singular, there are different positions among the grammarians on this. Some of the Kufan grammarians said: al-naʿam and al-anʿām are one thing, since both are plurals, so the pronoun in His words ﴿mimmā fī buṭūnihi﴾ was returned to the masculine, intending by it the meaning of al-naʿam, since it conveys the sense of al-anʿām, and he cited in support of this a rajaz by some Bedouin:

*Idhā raʾayta anjuman mina l-asad ... jabhatahu aw al-kharāt wal-katad ... bāla Suhayl fī l-faḍīkh fa-fasad ... wa-ṭāba albān al-liqāḥ fa-barad*

[The first three verses are in Lisān (jabah). al-Azharī said: al-jabha is the star called the forehead of the lion, four stars the moon alights on, the poet said: "idhā raʾayta..." In (Lisān: kharā) al-khurātān are two stars of the lion's constellation, two stars a whip's length apart, the two shoulders of the lion; the singular is khurāt, and he recited the four verses. In (Lisān: katad) al-katad is a star, Thaʿlab recited: "idhā raʾayta..." the verses. In (Lisān: suhl) al-Azharī said: Suhayl is a star not seen in Khurasan but seen in Iraq. Ibn Kunāsa said Suhayl is seen in the Ḥijāz and all over the land of the Arabs, but not seen in Armenia. al-Azharī said: Suhayl is a Yemeni star. In (Lisān: faḍkh) al-faḍīkh is grape juice, and it is also a drink made from unripe dates crushed alone without fire touching them, and it is the crushed one.

And faḍakhat al-busr and iftaḍakhathu means she crushed the dates; the rajiz said: "bāla Suhayl fī l-faḍīkh fa-fasad" meaning that when Suhayl rose the season of unripe dates passed and they ripened, as if it had urinated into it. The origin of these evidences is from al-Farrāʾ's evidences in Maʿānī al-Qurʾān; he said (p. 174): As for His words "mimmā fī buṭūnihi" and not "buṭūnihā," it was said, and God knows best, that al-naʿam and al-anʿām are one thing, both being plurals, so the masculine returned to the meaning of "al-naʿam," since it conveys the sense of al-anʿām. Some of them recited to me: "idhā raʾayta anjuman..." the four verses, which are of the mashṭūr rajaz. So the pronoun in His words "fayarudd" returned to milk, and milk and milks have one meaning. He said: al-Kisāʾī said "nusqīkum mimmā fī buṭūnihi": the bellies of what we mentioned. And that is correct. Some of them recited to me "mithl al-farākh nutifat ḥawāṣiluhu."]

He says: he returned with his words "fa-barad" to the meaning of milk, since milk and milks have one meaning. As for the masculine use of "naʿam," another poet said:

*Akulla ʿāmin naʿamun taḥwūnahu ... yulqiḥuhu qawmun wa-tantijūnahu*

[This rajaz is by Qays ibn al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Yazīd al-Ḥārithī, recited by Abū ʿUbayda in Majāz al-Qurʾān (1:362), who after the two verses of the evidence recited a third verse: "arbābuhu nawkā wa-lā yaḥmūnahu." The evidence in it is that al-anʿām is masculine and feminine. He said: others said the meaning is on al-naʿam, since al-naʿam is masculine and feminine. Lisān (naʿam) recited it: another said in the masculine use of al-naʿam: "fī kulli ʿāmin naʿamun yaḥwūnahu ... yulqiḥuhu qawmun wa-tantijūnahu." al-Baghdādī mentioned the rajaz in al-Khizāna (1:196-197) and added verses to it. He said: "wa-tantijūnahu" with the taʾ of address: it is said nataja al-nāqa ahluhā, when they cause her to bear young; anṭaja al-faras with the hamza: her time of foaling came; al-nitāj with a kasra is a name including the delivery of cattle, sheep and others. When a person helps a she-camel or ewe give birth until she delivers, it is said nataja-hā naṭjan (form ḍaraba), and the person is like the midwife, since he receives the offspring and sets its affairs right; he is nātij, the animal is manṭūja, and the young is natīja.

He says: they make the stallions cover the she-camels, and when they conceive, you then cause them to foal. The version of the verse in al-Khizāna is like the author's version. The verses were said on the day of al-Kilāb al-thānī, which is a water of Banū Tamīm between Kufa and Basra.] So he mentioned naʿam. Another of them said: he only said "mimmā fī buṭūnihi" because he meant: from what is in the bellies of what we mentioned, and he recites a rajaz by someone:

*Mithl al-firākh nutifat ḥawāṣiluhu*

[This is like the previous evidence, recited by al-Farrāʾ in Maʿānī al-Qurʾān (p. 174) as evidence that "nutifat ḥawāṣiluhu" means the crops of what we mentioned, as al-Kisāʾī explained. Ṣāḥib al-Lisān cited it in (naʿam) along with similar examples.]

And the verse of al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur:

*Inna l-maniyyata wal-ḥutūfa kilāhumā ... yūfī l-makhārima yarqubāni sawādī*

[The verse is by al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur al-Nahshalī al-Tamīmī (al-Mufaḍḍaliyyāt: 101). al-manniyya: death. al-ḥutūf: plural of ḥatf, meaning kinds of dangers that lead to death. al-makhārim: plural of mikhram, a rough path, according to al-Sukkarī; it is said: paths in the mountains and mouths of passes. sawād al-insān: his person. The evidence in the verse is his saying kilāhumā in the masculine, although al-manniyya and al-ḥutūf are feminine, and it should have been kiltāhumā, but the poet did not regard this feminine form and treated what the pronoun referred to earlier as two masculine things, meaning the two matters.]

So he said "kilāhumā" and did not say "kiltāhumā"; and the saying of al-Ṣalattān al-ʿAbdī:

*Inna l-samāḥata wal-murū'ata ḍumminā ... qabran bi-Marwa ʿalā l-ṭarīqi l-wāḍiḥi*

[The evidence in the verse is that al-samāḥa and al-murūʾa are two feminine words, yet the verb carrying their pronoun is not feminine. The poet said ḍumminā, not ḍummintā, because he regarded what the pronoun referred back to before the verb as two masculine things, or two natures, therefore the verb attributed to their pronoun was not made feminine.]

And the saying of another:

*Wa-ʿafrāʾu adnā al-nāsi minnī mawaddatan ... wa-ʿafrāʾu ʿannī l-muʿriḍu l-mutawānī*

[The author cited this verse as evidence that al-muʿriḍ, which is the predicate of ʿafrāʾ, did not agree with the subject ʿafrāʾ in feminineness, because the poet had in mind the meaning of the beloved or the person, which is masculine in meaning.]

He did not say "al-muʿriḍa al-mutawāniya." And the saying of another:

*Idhā l-nāsu nāsun wal-bilādu bighibṭatin ... wa-idh umm ʿAmmārin ṣadīqun musāʿifu*

[This evidence is like the previous one, since the poet took Umm ʿAmmār to mean a person, so he said ṣadīq by interpretation, not ṣadīqa by agreement. al-ṣadīq al-musāʿif: the one who draws close to his friend and aids him with his need.]

He says: all of that is according to the meaning of this thing, this person, and this person's form, and the like. He says: among that is the saying of God, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said: This is my Lord﴾ (6:78), meaning: this rising thing.

* *

His words ﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder, so whoever wills may remember it﴾ (74:54–55). He did not say "dhakarahā," because the meaning is: whoever wills, let him remember this thing.

* *

His words ﴿And indeed I am sending a gift to them, and I will wait to see with what the envoys return. So when he came to Solomon﴾ (27:35–36). He did not say "jāʾat." Some of the Basran grammarians said: it was said ﴿mimmā fī buṭūnihi﴾ because the meaning is: We give you to drink from whichever of the livestock has in its belly (that which) is milk; he says the word for milk is implied, meaning that from whichever of them has milk is what He gives to drink, since not all of them have milk, but drink is given only from those that have milk. The first two opinions are more sound in terms of Arabic usage than this third opinion.

* *

His words ﴿from between digestive contents and blood, pure milk﴾. He says: We give you milk, which We bring out for you from between digestive contents and blood, pure: it is pure of mixing with blood and digestive contents, so neither mixes with it ﴿palatable to those who drink﴾: it goes down smoothly for whoever drinks it, so he does not choke on it as a choker chokes on some of the food they eat. It is said: no one has ever choked on milk.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 16, Verse 67:

On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines, you take from them intoxicant and good provision. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reason.﴾

His Exalted remembrance says: And for you too, O people, there is a lesson in what We give you to drink from the fruits of the date palms and grapes: you take from them intoxicant and good provision, along with what We give you to drink from the bellies of livestock, the milk that comes out from between the waste and the blood. The noun has been omitted from His words ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines﴾, and the meaning is what I have described: "And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines, [there is something] you take from them," because the particle "min" (from/some of) indicates it, since "min" enters speech to indicate a part, so its indication and the listeners' knowledge of what the mention of the noun with it requires suffice. Some of the grammarians of Basra used to say regarding the meaning of the speech: "And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines there is a thing you take from it as intoxicant," and he said: the pronoun in His words ﴿you take from it﴾ was mentioned only because the thing is intended by it, and in our view it refers back to the omitted element, which is "ma" (that which).

* *

As for His words ﴿you take﴾:

It is an attribute of the omitted "ma".

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾. Some of them said: By "intoxicant" is meant wine, and by "good provision" is meant dates and raisins. They said: This verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine, and then it was prohibited afterward.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Ubayd al-Muharibi narrated to me, saying: Ayyub ibn Jabir al-Suhaymi narrated to us, from al-Aswad, from Amr ibn Sufyan, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: The intoxicant is what was forbidden of its drink, and the good provision is what was permitted of its fruit.

Ibn Wakic and Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' al-Razi narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Uyaynah narrated to us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Amr ibn Sufyan, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: The good provision is what was permitted of its fruit, and the intoxicant is what was forbidden of its fruit.

Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Aswad, from Amr ibn Sufyan, from Ibn Abbas, the like of it.

al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Amr ibn Sufyan, from Ibn Abbas, something similar.

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Amr ibn Sufyan, from Ibn Abbas, something similar.

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, who said: I heard a man narrating from Ibn Abbas concerning this verse, ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: The intoxicant is what was forbidden of their two fruits, and the good provision is what was permitted of their two fruits.

Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Salih narrated to us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Amr ibn Sufyan, from Ibn Abbas, something similar.

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Ghassan narrated to us, saying: Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiyah narrated to us, saying: al-Aswad ibn Qays narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Sufyan narrated to me, saying: I heard Ibn Abbas say, when this verse was mentioned in his presence ("And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines you take from them intoxicant and good provision"): The intoxicant is what was forbidden of them, and the good provision is what was permitted of them.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Sufyan informed us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri, who said: Ibn Abbas said, regarding His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: As for the good provision, it is what was permitted of their fruit, and as for the intoxicant, it is what was forbidden of their fruit.

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hammani informed us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from al-Aswad, from Amr ibn Sufyan al-Basri, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: The intoxicant: its forbidden part, and the good provision: its lawful part.

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Ubaydah informed us, saying: al-Abbas ibn Abi Talib narrated to us, saying: Abu Awanah narrated to us, from al-Aswad, from Amr ibn Sufyan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The intoxicant is what was forbidden of their fruit, and the good provision is what was made lawful of their fruit.

Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The good provision is the lawful, and the intoxicant is the unlawful.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: What was forbidden of their fruit, and what was permitted of their fruit.

Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The intoxicant is wine, and the good provision is the lawful.

Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Mis'ar and Sufyan, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The good provision is the lawful, and the intoxicant is the unlawful.

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, something similar.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding this verse, ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: The intoxicant is the unlawful, and the good provision is the lawful.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Abu Razin, regarding ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: This was revealed while they were drinking wine, and this was before the prohibition of wine was revealed.

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim, al-Sha'bi and Abu Razin, who said: It is abrogated by this verse, ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾.

al-Hasan ibn Arafah narrated to us, saying: Abu Qatan narrated to us, from Sa'id, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim and al-Sha'bi, and Abu Razin, something similar.

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Awn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim, regarding His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: It is abrogated; the prohibition of wine abrogated it.

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hawdhah narrated to us, saying: Awf narrated to us, from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: God mentioned His blessing in the intoxicant before the prohibition of wine.

al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Awn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Mansur and Awf, from al-Hasan, who said: The intoxicant is what God forbade of it, and the provision is what God made lawful of it.

Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from al-Hasan, who said: The good provision is the lawful, and the intoxicant is the unlawful.

Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Salamah, from al-Dahhak, who said: The good provision is the lawful, and the intoxicant is the unlawful.

Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Abu Kudaynah Yahya ibn al-Muhallab, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: The intoxicant is wine, and the good provision is the ripe dates and grapes.

Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿you take from it intoxicant﴾, he said: It is wine before it was prohibited.

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us; and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿you take from it intoxicant﴾, he said: Wine before its prohibition; ﴿and good provision﴾, he said: food.

al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, something similar.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines you take from them intoxicant and good provision﴾: As for the intoxicant, it is the wines of these non-Arabs; as for the good provision, it is what you make into nabidh, what you make into vinegar, and what you eat. This verse was revealed while wine had not yet been prohibited that day; its prohibition came afterward in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Ubaydah ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I read to Ibn Abi Udhrah, who said: Thus I heard Qatadah [recite] ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, then he mentioned something like the narration of Bishr.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿intoxicant﴾, he said: It is the wines of the non-Arabs, and it was abrogated in Surat al-Ma'idah; and the good provision, he said: what you make into nabidh, what you make into vinegar, and what you eat.

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines you take from them intoxicant and good provision﴾: This is because the people used to call wine "intoxicant," and they used to drink it. Ibn Abbas said [[The words "Ibn Abbas said" up to "they return from it" are as they stand in the manuscripts. It seems inserted into the middle of the speech, and al-Suyuti dropped it from al-Durr al-Manthur when he related this hadith.]] Men passed by the valley of al-Sakran, where Quraysh used to gather when they met their travelers coming from al-Sham, and they went with them, escorting them until they reached the valley of al-Sakran, and then they returned from it. Then God later named it "wine" when it was prohibited. Ibn Abbas used to claim that it was wine, and he used to claim that the Abyssinians call vinegar "sakar."

* *

His words ﴿and good provision﴾

He means by this: the lawful, dates and raisins, and whatever was lawful that does not intoxicate.

Others said: "Intoxicant" is in the same position as wine regarding prohibition, though it is not wine; they said it is the infusion of dates and raisins when it ferments and comes to intoxicate its drinker.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, regarding His words ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines you take from them intoxicant and good provision﴾, Ibn Abbas said: This was before the prohibition of wine was revealed, and intoxicant is forbidden like wine; as for its lawful part, it is raisins, dates, vinegar, and the like.

al-Muthanna and Ali ibn Dawud narrated to me, both saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant﴾: then God forbade, after that, meaning after what was revealed in Surat al-Baqarah mentioning wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows, the intoxicant along with the prohibition of wine, because it is from it. He said ﴿and good provision﴾: it is the lawful from vinegar, nabidh, and the like, so God affirmed it and made it lawful for the Muslims.

Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Musa, who said: I once asked about the intoxicant, and he said: Abd Allah said: it is wine.

Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Farwah, from Abu Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: The intoxicant is wine.

Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu al-Haytham, from Ibrahim, who said: The intoxicant is wine.

Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Salih narrated to us, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim and Abu Razin, who both said: The intoxicant is wine.

I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant﴾: meaning whatever intoxicates of grapes and dates, ﴿and good provision﴾: meaning their fruit.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾: The lawful is what was in the lawful manner, until they altered it and made from it intoxicant.

Others said: "Intoxicant" is whatever is lawful to drink, such as lawful nabidh, vinegar, and ripe dates. And "good provision" is dates and raisins.

Mention of those who said that:

Dawud al-Wasiti narrated to me, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, Abu Rawq said: I narrated to me, saying: I said to al-Sha'bi: Have you seen His words ﴿you take from it intoxicant﴾: is it this intoxicant that the Nabat make? He said: No, this is wine. The intoxicant that God the Exalted mentioned is nabidh and vinegar, and the good provision is dates and raisins.

Yahya ibn Dawud narrated to me, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, saying: and Mujalid mentioned, from Amir, something similar.

Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Mandal narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿you take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾, he said: What they used to make from the palm was nabidh, and the good provision is what they used to make from raisins and dates.

Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Mandal narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Sha'bi, who said: I said to him: What do you make from it as intoxicant? He said: They used to make it from nabidh and vinegar. I said: And the good provision? He said: They used to make it from dates and raisins.

Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah and Ahmad ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, who said: The intoxicant is nabidh, and the good provision is the dates that were eaten; and according to this interpretation, the verse is not abrogated, but its ruling remains.

This interpretation, in my view, is the most preferable of the sayings for the interpretation of this verse. The reason is that "sakar" in the speech of the Arabs has four senses. The first: what intoxicates of drink. The second: what is eaten of food, as the poet said:

"I made the faults of the noble a sakar (a relish)"

That is, a food. The third: calm, from the saying of the poet:

"I made the eye of the scorching heat become sakar (subside)"

That is, its heat quiets and fades. And it is said: a sakirah night, meaning a calm night. And the fourth: the verbal noun from the saying: "Fulan sakara, yaskaru, sukran and sakran and sakaran." So if this is so, and what intoxicates of drink is unlawful by what we have shown in our book entitled "Latif al-Qawl fi Ahkam Shara'i al-Islam," and it is not permissible for us to say that it is abrogated, since the abrogated is that whose ruling the abrogating one negates, and it is impossible for its ruling and its abrogator to coexist; and there was in God the Exalted's prohibition of wine no proof that the sakar which is other than wine, and other than what intoxicates of drink, is unlawful, since sakar is one of its meanings among the Arabs, and the one to whom the Qur'an was revealed in his tongue means by it everything that is eaten; and since there was in the revelation itself no proof that it is abrogated, nor did a report from the Messenger say that it is abrogated, nor did the community agree upon it, it is necessary to say what we have said: that the meaning of "sakar" in this place is whatever is lawful to drink, made from the fruit of the palm and the vine; and it is invalid that its meaning be wine or what intoxicates of drink, and it has departed from being the sakar itself, since sakar is not something made from palms and vines, and from being in the sense of calm.

* *

His words ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reason﴾

He says: In what We have described to you of Our blessings which We have bestowed upon you, O people, of livestock, date palms and vines, there is clear proof and a manifest sign for a people who reason about God's proofs, and understand from Him His admonitions, so that they take heed by them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 68:

The explanation of His words: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee: "Take for yourself houses in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they build."﴾

He, may He be exalted, says: And your Lord inspired (alhama) the bee with an inspiration (iyha') to it: ﴿Take for yourself houses in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they build﴾, meaning: in what they build of roofs, which they raise by construction.

Concerning this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Yaqub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Marwan related to us, from Ishaq al-Tamimi, who is Ibn Abi al-Sabbah, from a man, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾: he said, "He inspired it with inspiration (ilham)."

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: It reached me, concerning His words ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾: he said, "He cast it into their souls (qadhafa fi anfusiha)."

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Abu Sufyan related to me, from Ma'mar, from his companions, regarding His words ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾: he said, "He cast into their souls: take for yourselves houses in the mountains."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ ... to the end of the verse, he said: "He commanded it to eat from the fruits, and commanded it to follow the paths of its Lord, made easy (dhululan)."

We have already explained the meaning of inspiration (al-iha') and the differences of those who differ about it, earlier, with its evidences, in a way that suffices without repeating it in this place. Likewise the meaning of His words ﴿they build (ya'rishun)﴾.

Ibn Zayd used to say concerning the meaning of "ya'rishun" what follows:

- It was related to me by Yunus, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words ﴿ya'rishun﴾: "It is the vineyard (al-karm)."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 69:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Then eat of all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy (dhulul).  From their bellies emerges a drink of varying colours, in which there is healing for mankind. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾ (69)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Then eat, O bee, from all the fruits, ﴿and follow the ways of your Lord﴾, meaning: follow the paths of your Lord ﴿made easy (dhulul)﴾, meaning: made smooth for you. The dhulul is the plural of dhalul (easy, tractable).

In accordance with what we have said on this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have spoken.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to us, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us. And al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us. And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, from Warqa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God, the Exalted, ﴿and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy﴾, he said: No place she has traversed becomes rough for her.

- Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, ﴿and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy﴾, he said: paths made easy; no place she has traversed becomes rough for her. And according to this interpretation which Mujahid gave, dhulul is a description of the paths (al-subul).

The interpretation of His saying ﴿follow the ways of your Lord, made easy﴾, with dhulul meaning for you: no path you have travelled becomes rough for you. Then the alif and lam were dropped and it was put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Others said regarding this:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿follow the ways of your Lord, made easy﴾: meaning obedient.

- Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, ﴿dhulul﴾, he said: obedient.

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿follow the ways of your Lord, made easy﴾: The dhalul is that which is led and taken wherever its owner wishes. He said: They take the bees out, seeking pasture with them, and they go, and the bees follow them. And he recited ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle, and they are their owners? And We made them tractable (dhallalnaha) for them﴾ ... the verse. According to this view, dhulul is a description of the bees. Both opinions are not far from the correct, and each has a valid line of explanation; however, we have chosen that it is a description of the paths, since it is closer to them.

And His saying ﴿From their bellies emerges a drink of varying colours﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: From the bellies of the bees emerges a drink, which is honey, of varying colours, for among them are white, red, and asḥar, and other colours.

Abu Ja'far said: asḥar: varying colours, such as white tending towards red.

And His saying ﴿in which there is healing for mankind﴾

The people of interpretation differed concerning what the pronoun in His saying ﴿fīhi (in it)﴾ refers back to. Some said it refers to the Qur'an, and that is what is meant by it.

Those who said this:

- Nasr ibn Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: al-Muharibi related to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, ﴿in which there is healing for mankind﴾, he said: in the Qur'an is healing.

Others said: Rather, what is meant is honey.

Those who said this:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿From their bellies emerges a drink of varying colours, in which there is healing for mankind﴾: in it is healing from illnesses, as God said. And he used to forbid separating the bees and killing them.

- Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that his brother had a complaint of the stomach. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go and give your brother honey to drink." Then he came back and said: It has only increased him in severity. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go and give your brother honey to drink, for God has spoken the truth and your brother's belly has lied." So he gave him to drink, and it was as if he had been released from a fetter.

- Al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, ﴿From their bellies emerges a drink of varying colours, in which there is healing for mankind﴾, he said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned something similar.

- Ibn Waki' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abdullah, who said: There are two healings: honey is a healing from every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾: it is honey.

This opinion, namely the opinion of Qatada, is more appropriate as the interpretation of the verse, because His saying "fīhi" occurs in the context of a report about honey, so that the pronoun refers to the mention of honey is more fitting than anything else, since it stands in the context of the report about it.

And His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed in God's bringing forth from the bellies of these bees a varying drink, which is healing for mankind, is a clear proof and evidence for whoever subjected the bees and guided them to eat the fruits they eat, and to take for themselves houses hewn from mountains, trees and trellises, and brought forth from their bellies what He brought forth of healing for mankind, that He is the One, there is nothing like Him, and that it is not fitting that He have a partner, and divinity is valid only for Him.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah created you, then causes you to die; and among you is he who is brought back to the most abject old age, so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing. Indeed Allah is Knowing, Competent.﴾ (16:70)**

He, the Exalted, says: And Allah created you, O people, and brought you into existence when you were nothing, not the deities you worship besides Him. So worship the One who created you, not other than Him. ﴿Then causes you to die﴾: that is, then He takes you back. ﴿And among you is he who is brought back to the most abject old age﴾: that is, among you is one who grows senile and reaches "the most abject old age," which is its worst state. It is said of it: the man became abject (radhula) and worthless (fasula), he becomes abject, with the verbal noun radhala and radhula, and I made him abject (radhaltuhu). It was said: he reaches that state at seventy-five years.

Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Fazari narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Sawwar informed us, saying: Asad ibn Imran narrated to us, from Sa'd ibn Tarif, from al-Asbagh ibn Nubata, from Ali, concerning His saying ﴿and among you is he who is brought back to the most abject old age﴾, that he said: "Seventy-five years."

* *

And His saying ﴿so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing﴾:

That is: We only bring him back to the most abject old age so that he returns to ignorance as he was in his childhood and youth, so that after having knowledge he knows nothing; that is, so that he does not know anything after a knowledge he had in his youth. That knowledge is taken away by old age, he forgets, and nothing of it is known to him, and his reason departs from him, so that after having reason he does not understand anything. ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing, Competent﴾: that is, Allah does not forget, and His knowledge does not change; He knows all that was and all that will be, and He is Capable of whatever He wills, He is not ignorant of anything, and nothing He intends can overcome Him.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. Yet those who are favoured do not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they are equal in it. Is it then the grace of Allah that they deny?﴾ (16:71)

He, the Exalted, says: And Allah, O people, has favoured some of you over others in the provision He has given you in this world. So those whom Allah has favoured over others in what He has provided them ﴿do not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess﴾: that is, they do not give to their slaves who are associates (mushrikin) in their property and wives, what He has provided them of wealth and spouses. ﴿So that they are equal in it﴾: that is, so that they and their slaves are equal in that. He, the Exalted, says: They do not consent to be, they and their slaves, equal in what I have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and authority. This is a parable God, the Exalted, has struck for those who associate others with Allah. It was also said: it refers only to those Christians who said that the Messiah is the son of Allah.

* *

And His saying ﴿Is it then the grace of Allah that they deny?﴾:

He, the Exalted, says: Is it then the grace of Allah, which He has bestowed upon these polytheists in the provision He has given them in this world, that they deny by associating with Allah some of His creation in His authority and dominion?

Those of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah created you, then causes you to die; and among you is he who is brought back to the most abject old age, so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing. Indeed Allah is Knowing, Competent.﴾ (16:70)**

He, the Exalted, says: And Allah created you, O people, and brought you into existence when you were nothing, not the deities you worship besides Him. So worship the One who created you, not other than Him. ﴿Then causes you to die﴾: that is, then He takes you back. ﴿And among you is he who is brought back to the most abject old age﴾: that is, among you is one who grows senile and reaches "the most abject old age," which is its worst state. It is said of it: the man became abject (radhula) and worthless (fasula), he becomes abject, with the verbal noun radhala and radhula, and I made him abject (radhaltuhu). It was said: he reaches that state at seventy-five years.

Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Fazari narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Sawwar informed us, saying: Asad ibn Imran narrated to us, from Sa'd ibn Tarif, from al-Asbagh ibn Nubata, from Ali, concerning His saying ﴿and among you is he who is brought back to the most abject old age﴾, that he said: "Seventy-five years."

* *

And His saying ﴿so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing﴾:

That is: We only bring him back to the most abject old age so that he returns to ignorance as he was in his childhood and youth, so that after having knowledge he knows nothing; that is, so that he does not know anything after a knowledge he had in his youth. That knowledge is taken away by old age, he forgets, and nothing of it is known to him, and his reason departs from him, so that after having reason he does not understand anything. ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing, Competent﴾: that is, Allah does not forget, and His knowledge does not change; He knows all that was and all that will be, and He is Capable of whatever He wills, He is not ignorant of anything, and nothing He intends can overcome Him.

He, the Exalted, says: They do not consent to be, they and their slaves, equal in what I have provided them, yet they have made My servants partners in My dominion and authority. This is a parable God, the Exalted, has struck for those who associate others with Allah. It was also said: it refers only to those Christians who said that the Messiah is the son of Allah.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 16, verse 72:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has made for you from yourselves spouses, and has made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren (ḥafadah), and provided for you of the good things. Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the favour of Allah do they disbelieve?﴾ (16:72)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿And Allah﴾ who ﴿has made for you﴾, O people, ﴿from yourselves spouses﴾, meaning that He created Eve, his wife, from Adam. ﴿And has made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren (ḥafadah)﴾.

As related:

• Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And Allah has made for you from yourselves spouses﴾: that is, Allah created Adam, then created his wife from him, then made for you sons and ḥafadah.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding who is meant by al-ḥafadah. Some of them said: they are the in-laws, the sons-in-law of a man through his daughters.

ḥafada al-walā'idu ḥawlahunna wa-uslimat ... bi-akuffihinna azimmatu al-ajmāl [[The verse was cited shortly before on page 144; refer to it there.]]

He said: and slaves cannot be among the spouses; how could a slave come from my wife? Rather al-ḥafadah are a man's sons and his servants.
